#91748. Is Your Cycling Computer Lying to You?

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1294 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bicycling ↗ Open Full Page

Is Your Cycling Computer Lying to You?

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1294 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Spend enough time comparing power meters, and you’ll promptly learn that they don’t always agree.
  • In a recent development, if you use a power meter for training, what matters most is that the numbers you’re seeing today are comparable to the ones you saw last week or last month.
  • But what if your power meter isn’t the only thing affecting those numbers?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Spend enough time comparing power meters, and you’ll promptly learn that they don’t always agree. Put a power meter on your crank and another on your pedals, and the numbers may not match exactly. That can be frustrating when you’re trying to figure out which one is right, but for most riders, a small, consistent difference isn’t necessarily a problem.

In a recent development, if you use a power meter for training, what matters most is that the numbers you’re seeing today are comparable to the ones you saw last week or last month. Whether your threshold is actually 250 watts or 255 watts matters less than knowing that an interval at that power represents the same effort from one ride to the next.

But what if your power meter isn’t the only thing affecting those numbers? What if the bike computer recording your ride is changing the data before you ever upload it to Strava or TrainingPeaks?

Recent findings suggest that I recently noticed something odd while testing a cycling computer. At first, I was doing this to compare GPS track accuracy, but since I was testing, I also paired all the devices to my heart rate strap and Quarq power meter. When I compared the ride files afterward, what stood out was that their power numbers didn’t match. Initially, the differences were small enough. But when I looked more closely, I noticed it immediately. Every time I stopped pedaling, one computer still recorded power.

Recent findings suggest that before I get into what the heck sticky watts are, I should say I first learned about the issue in 2025 when I saw a video from Shane Miller, who goes by GPLama on YouTube. The video is called “Power Meter Data Recording: The Wild West?”, and it’s worth watching. Shane was the first person I saw digging into this particular recording issue with cycling computers.

Sources indicate that so what the heck is it? Sticky watts happen when a cycling computer keeps recording a power value for a few seconds after you’ve stopped pedaling. Instead of dropping to zero, the last power number gets “stuck” in your ride file until the computer finally catches up.

Let’s say you’re riding along at 250 watts and stop pedaling as you approach a corner. Your computer might continue recording 250 watts for a few seconds while you’re coasting. On a graph, that can look like a flat line extending beyond the point where the power should have dropped.

According to recent reports, A few seconds might not sound like much, but think about how often you stop pedaling on a typical ride. Every corner, descent, stop sign, or moment spent coasting in the group is another opportunity for those extra watts to show up in your file. And if you stop pedaling after a hard effort, the computer could be holding a much higher number than 250 watts, which can skew your data.

It’s also worth distinguishing this from the setting on some computers that lets you exclude zeroes when calculating average power. That setting changes how an average is calculated. Sticky watts affect the power values recorded in the ride file itself, so those extra values can still be there when you upload the ride for analysis.

In a recent development, on one ride, I compared the DURA 2 with a Garmin Edge 850 and an Edge 1060. The two Garmins recorded almost identical power numbers, but the DURA 2 consistently came out higher. When I looked more closely at the files, I found repeated instances where the COROS continued recording the last power value after both Garmins had dropped to zero.

The difference was especially noticeable during a series of short, hard efforts. After one effort, the DURA 2 recorded 565 watts for four seconds while both Garmins recorded zero. After another, it held 656 watts for three seconds. Across a roughly three-minute section containing several of these efforts, the Garmins averaged about 260 watts, while the COROS recorded nearly 307 watts.

Recent findings suggest that those short efforts make the glitch easy to see, but the difference revealed up across the ride, too. In the roughly 98 minutes of matched power data I compared, the DURA 2 averaged about 186 watts, while both Garmins averaged about 179 watts.

Sources indicate that on a second ride, I compared the DURA 2 with a Hammerhead Karoo, Wahoo ELEMNT ACE, and Garmin Edge 850. Again, the COROS recorded higher power through a section with several hard efforts followed by coasting. The Garmin recorded lower numbers than the Karoo and Wahoo in that section, which reminds us that differences can go both ways when computers record the same power meter.

It has been revealed that I was honestly surprised to see this on the DURA 2. The original DURA had similar problems early on, but its power recording improved with subsequent updates, and it performed well in GPLama’s 2025 video presenting the problem. I don’t want to turn this into a story about picking on COROS. The organization has a good history of updating and improving its products, and I expect it can address this issue on the DURA 2 as well. For now, these files show why it’s worth paying attention to what your cycling computer records, even when you trust your power meter.

If you mostly ride for fun and don’t pay much attention to your power data afterward, a few extra watts in your ride file probably won’t change your life. But if you use that data to track your training, compare rides, and work with a coach, those differences can matter.

The significant problem is that sticky watts don’t necessarily add the same amount to every ride. A steady climb with little coasting might show no difference. But a ride with lots of corners, stop signs, descents, or short, hard efforts followed by coasting could produce a much larger one. That makes it harder to compare rides or judge how much work you actually did.

The easiest way to check is to record the same ride on two cycling computers paired to the same power meter. You don’t necessarily need to buy a second computer. If a friend has one you can borrow, pair both to your power meter and record a ride with a few clear transitions from pedaling to coasting.

Alternatively, you can look closely at the power files your head unit generates. Do a couple of hard efforts, like sprints, where you stop pedaling at the end, then zoom in on those sections. Look for a flat section where one computer continues recording the same power value for several seconds after the other has dropped to zero.

In a recent development, and yes, I know that I’m definitely in some deep weeds over here, and it can be tough to argue that a cycling computer recording a few extra watts is a huge problem worth tackling. For many riders, it might not matter at all. But the current crop of cycling computers is also the most expensive we’ve ever seen. These devices are marketed and sold as precision training tools, and accurate data recording is central to that. These devices should do that, and riders shouldn’t have to question it.

Test Editor Dan Chabanov got his start in cycling as a New York City bike messenger but quickly found his way into road and cyclocross racing, competing in professional cyclocross races from 2009 to 2019 and winning a Master’s National Championship title in 2018. Prior to joining Bicycling in 2021, Dan worked as part of the race organization for the Red Hook Crit, as a coach with EnduranceWERX, as well as a freelance writer and photographer.

Picture this: you're seated in a private suite at 38,000 feet somewhere over the Atlantic, your door clicked shut behind you, a glass of Dom Pérignon on the side table, and a fully flat bed dressed in Westin Heavenly bedding waiting for you. Your partner is in the suite next to yours — and when you lower the center dividing panel, you're sharing a meal in what Qatar Airways calls the "Double Bed" configuration. This is QSuites, and it is, without exaggeration, the single most celebrated business class product in the world. Now here's the number that stops the ChooseFI community cold: a cash ticket in QSuites from New York JFK to Doha DOH typically runs **$5,000 to $10,000 per person**. That's a mortgage payment. That's a family vacation budget. That's real money that compounds in an index fund. With Qatar Avios through the Privilege Club program, that same seat costs **75,000 Avios**. When you do the math against even the conservative cash price of $5,000, you're extracting **6.7 cents per point**. Against the top-end cash price of $10,000, that's **13.3 cents per point** — in a world where most loyalty currencies are "worth" 1 cent each. This is a 6x to 13x multiplier on every point you've earned. Here's what makes this a genuine pricing inefficiency rather than just marketing: Qatar's award chart is fixed and partner-friendly, meaning the number of points required doesn't scale dynamically with cash prices the way most airline programs now do. When demand spikes and cash fares hit $10,000, your award price stays exactly 75,000 Avios. The loyalty program hasn't caught up to the revenue management engine, and that gap is your opportunity. For anyone on the path to financial independence, this is the travel rewards philosophy in its purest form: redirect real spending you're already doing onto the right cards, accumulate points as a byproduct, and convert those points into experiences that would otherwise require liquidating investments. The QSuites redemption is the pinnacle of that system — a **nearly free** business class experience that delivers more luxury per point than almost anything else in the world of travel rewards.

The mechanism behind this sweet spot is elegant once you see it, and once you see it, you'll start recognizing similar patterns everywhere in the loyalty space.

Qatar prices its own flights in its own currency — and that currency is cheap to acquire.

Sources indicate that qatar Airways Privilege Club Avios are the program's native points currency. When Qatar sets award prices for its own operated flights, including QSuites, it prices them in a way that's competitive and fixed — not subject to the dynamic pricing algorithms that have made programs like United MileagePlus or Delta SkyMiles increasingly unpredictable. Seventy-five thousand Avios for a transatlantic or transoceanic business class seat is a published, stable price. Qatar isn't trying to extract maximum value from every award booking; they want to keep the program attractive to drive loyalty.

In a recent development, the critical insight is this: you don't need to earn Qatar Avios through Qatar flights. You can transfer them directly from credit card programs you're probably already using.

Citi ThankYou Points → Qatar Avios at 1:1 — This is the fastest and cleanest route. Transfers from Citi to Qatar are instant, meaning you can search for availability, confirm the seat is bookable, and transfer in the same session without risk. For anyone holding a Citi Premier or Citi Prestige card, this is a direct pipeline to QSuites.

Capital One Miles → Qatar Avios at 1:1 — A strong secondary option. Capital One's transfer to Qatar takes 2–5 days, so you'll want to confirm availability first and ideally put the seat on a 24-hour hold if possible before initiating the transfer. Venture X and Venture card holders have access to this path.

Sources indicate that marriott Bonvoy Points → Qatar Avios at 3:1 — This is the least efficient path. The 3:1 ratio means you're effectively diluting your Bonvoy points, and transfers take 1–5 days. Use this only as a top-off strategy if you're a few thousand Avios short and have Bonvoy points sitting idle.

This is a huge deal that deserves its own callout. Qatar charges zero fuel surcharges on Qatar-operated award flights. This is not universal — British Airways Avios, for example, can pile on $700+ in carrier-imposed surcharges on longhaul awards. With Qatar Privilege Club, what you see is what you pay: 75,000 Avios plus the government taxes, which are typically modest.

Qatar allows stopovers in Doha and open-jaw routing on award tickets. This means you can build a trip that stops in Doha — giving you access to the Al Mourjan Business Lounge, one of the world's premier airport lounges — before continuing to a final destination. The stopover rule turns a single award redemption into a multi-destination experience, a classic FI travel rewards optimization move.

This is the cardinal rule of all transfer-based award bookings: never transfer points until you've confirmed the seat exists. Go to qatarairways.com and run a search using the "Privilege Club" award booking tool. Select Business Class, enter your route (e.g., JFK to DOH), and look for QSuites availability specifically — you'll see the aircraft type and cabin configuration in the search results. QSuites is typically available on Boeing 777-300ER and A380 flights, not all Qatar aircraft, so confirm the product before you get excited.

Recent findings suggest that qatar Privilege Club opens its award booking window at 361 days in advance. QSuites availability is genuinely limited — this is a Difficulty 2/5 on the availability scale — and the best seats disappear swiftly, especially for peak travel periods and popular routes like JFK–DOH. Set a calendar reminder now for exactly 361 days before your target departure date and be ready to book the moment the window opens. This single habit separates people who get QSuites awards from people who watch them disappear.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

If a cyclist is able to work strength training into their fitness routine, especially throughout the off-season, then the ceiling for potential power and speed goes up. The challenge is, as cyclists we just want to ride our bikes—driving to a gym, spending an hour or more in the weight room, then driving home is that much less time we’ll get in the saddle.

I’ve spent close to the last decade as a personal trainer, and there is one piece of equipment I have come to prioritize in my home gym—no matter the season. The TRX Suspension Strap System is a versatile, compact, and burlier-than-expected piece of gym equipment. I’ve had the same pair since I was certified almost 10 years ago and they are still in great shape—even after loads of personal use as well as using them for in-home training sessions with clients.

In a recent development, one of the major reasons I continue to use the TRX system in my own workouts is because I can do a full-body strength workout, in a fraction of the time it takes me in the weight room, and I can do it all with one piece of equipment at home. All the TRX system needs is a way to mount it and enough room to do the exercises on the list.

Here, we’ll dig deeper into what TRX Suspension Straps are, why I recommend them to cyclists specifically, and give you a workout to jumpstart your season.

TRX Suspension Straps are a suspension-based training tool designed to be used for bodyweight exercises. They were initially created by Randy Hetrick, a former U.S. Navy SEAL. He wanted to create a piece of fitness equipment that could offer full-body training and fit into a backpack—several iterations later, TRX was born. TRX Suspension Straps are basically a set of adjustable nylon straps that have handles to grab and cradles for feet. Most of the exercises you start with will have both hands on the handles, but as you progress you will start to add exercises with your feet in the cradles instead. The unique thing about this piece of equipment is that it can equally push a high-level athlete as well as offer things like balance improvement exercises. TRX bands can take simple exercises like a plank or a squat and offer modifications to make the exercise easier or create challenging progressions to make the exercise (much) harder. That makes them valuable for cyclists just starting out on a strength-training program or for those of us who have been doing it for years. The other great thing is they pack down really well. I have personally put them in the bottom of a carry-on bag on many trips over the years. You can set them up on everything from a traditional wall anchor to tree limbs and doorjambs. During my in-home personal training days, I had even set them up poolside for a great outdoor session with a client.

Cyclists benefit from some level of strength training off the bike. It’s one of the best ways to build speed, power, and durability. (Our Strength Training for Cyclists program, which is free to members, is packed with training plans, strategies, and expert advice, making it a great place to get started or to elevate your current workouts.) With the TRX system, you can get all the benefits of strength training in with a tool that’s super effective. I like it because you can use it for moves that work your whole body, like an atomic push-up, which is when you perform a pushup with your feet in the bands, or something that isolates a muscle group, like a calf raise. Building a strong and sound core is a key to developing stability through the body.

One great thing about the TRX straps is that almost every exercise you do will help improve core stability. Increasing that stability will allow for better energy transfer through your body as you ride. The straps also are incredible for mobility and stretching, allowing you to get deeper into and out of stretches. They do this by allowing you an extra point of stability when your hands are holding the handles or cradles at the end of the straps.

If you are setting these up in your home gym, you will need a way to mount the straps. They come with a carabiner attached to the straps, but that has to get clipped to something. I typically use a double-length nylon sling used for climbing because I had a few of these lying around that I retired from my climbing rack. TRX also makes specific straps, wall anchors, and even doorjamb anchors to set the straps up on just about anything you can think of. Pro tip—make sure the anchor you use for the straps is strong enough to hold more than bodyweight.

It has been revealed that I have been using my own set of the TRX Straps for over a decade now and they show few signs of wear. During my time as a personal trainer, I used the suspension straps for everyone from elite athletes to people in their seventies and eighties just looking to improve balance and mobility. They can handle everything from explosive training days to core and stability training. For cyclists that are looking to build a stronger core, here are a few of my favorite exercises.

It has been revealed that you can find our complete expert-recommended workout here. The exercises, demonstrated by Susane Pata, TRX senior master instructor, will build the strength, stability, and mobility cyclists need. You can do the warmup moves anytime you want to wake up your muscles before a ride, and the stretches to loosen up when you’re done.

  • In a recent development, when you run, the QL plays more of a stabilizing role, working to control your pelvis and trunk while you stride, says Spencer Agnew, PT, DPT, a physical therapist at Sword Health and run coach with Wisconsin-based Ascent Endurance Group.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that most runners are familiar with the massive muscles involved in running, such as the quads, hamstrings, and glutes. But there are lesser-known—yet still vital—players that can influence running performance. One example: the quadratus lumborum, or QL for short.

A deep trunk muscle, the QL attaches to the lower spine and the back side of the pelvis, Nicole Haas, PT, DPT, a physical therapist and founder of Boulder Physiolab in Colorado, tells Runner’s World. It serves a few different functions in daily life, such as helping you arch your back, bend to the side, and rotate your upper body, Haas explains.

In a recent development, when you run, the QL plays more of a stabilizing role, working to control your pelvis and trunk while you stride, says Spencer Agnew, PT, DPT, a physical therapist at Sword Health and run coach with Wisconsin-based Ascent Endurance Group. The QL also assists with breathing, specifically when you inhale, Agnew adds.

Recent findings suggest that if this muscle is tight or irritated, you’ll likely feel pain in your back or sacroiliac joints, which link the pelvis and lower spine, Agnew notes. To help you avoid these aches, we asked the PTs to explain what can cause an angry QL and how to relieve it.

There are several reasons your QL might be yelling at you. A common one? Your hip flexors are tight. In particular, when the psoas (a massive, rope-like hip flexor muscle that runs from your lower back to the front of your hip) is shortened, it can pull your pelvis into an anterior tilt, meaning your pelvis is tipped forward, arching your lower back. In many cases, this yanks on your QL as well, because the psoas and QL both insert into the same group of vertebrae in your lower back, Agnew explains.

In a recent development, another culprit is weak glutes. When your glutes aren’t strong enough to help you maintain good running mechanics, your knee can collapse inward as you land and your opposite-side hip can dip down, Haas explains. This, in turn, can cause your trunk to side bend and rotate, thus placing more strain on your QL over time. Running downhill can exacerbate the problem, Haas adds, because that can cause your lower back to arch and place further stress on your QL.

Recent findings suggest that yet another cause of an irritated QL is upper-back stiffness. Restrictions in the upper part of the spine can shift more workload onto the QL, Haas explains. So can challenges in your shoulders, hips, and mid-back. If these areas aren’t moving like they should due to pain or injury, your QL may receive added stress, Haas indicates.

Keep in mind that in some cases, your QL may hurt because it’s taking on a bunch of extra stress it’s not meant to, but the muscle itself probably isn’t tight. “It’s more like your QL is just irritated because everything has been collapsing around it and loading it,” Haas states. “It’s overworked and underappreciated.”.

It has been revealed that A tight-feeling QL is worth addressing because it can lead to a few not-so-great issues if left unchecked. A massive one? Compromised running mechanics.

A tight QL, as mentioned, can shorten your hip flexors and pull your pelvis into an anterior tilt, which will reduce your knee lift as you stride, Agnew says. As a result, “you’re not going to be able to generate as much force moving forward, and you’ll have more of an arched-back position when you run,” he explains. In many cases, this can deliver a double whammy of reduced performance and increased back pain, he says.

On top of that, a tight QL can also hinder your breathing. As mentioned above, one of the QL’s jobs is to help you inhale, so when this muscle is tight, you may not be able to breathe as deeply or easily, Agnew states.

In a recent development, plagued by what you think may be an irritated QL? Try Agnew’s three-step at-home series to help reduce your discomfort.

Perform this sequence as often as every day if you’re in significant discomfort that’s limiting your ability to run. In the case of minor pain, incorporate this series two to three times per week. On the days you run, perform the myofascial release, pelvic tilts, and hip hikes before you lace up, then tackle the other components afterward.

This can help turn down the pain response in a barking QL by desensitizing soft tissue, Agnew explains.

How to Perform Myofascial Release.

It has been revealed that the pelvic tilts help you learn how to coordinate and control pelvic motion so you can maintain proper mechanics while running, and the hip hikes help activate your QL. The kettlebell side bend increases blood flow to the muscle, which can aid in healing. Finally, the suitcase carry increases strength, stability, and engagement of the muscle, which can ensure it functions properly during a run.

Lengthen your QL—as well as tight hip flexors—with this two-for-one half-kneeling lunge stretch.

Sources indicate that do these moves daily or several times per day to mobilize your lower back. Perform them before or after a run. Crucial caveat: If your QL hurts more after stretching—or if your QL pain returns soon after stretching—then stretches are likely not the solution and you should stop doing them, Haas explains.

Dynamic QL Mobility + Hip 90/90.

It has been revealed that to start, do one set of these moves daily to help your body learn the neuromuscular patterns. (The caveat: If you feel sore, then skip a day.) After about six weeks, do these moves two to three times per week as part of your regular strength-training routine.

This exercise targets the glutes and works on pelvic control in a movement pattern that’s similar to running. Think of it as an opportunity to train proper glute use in your running form, which will help unload any strain on your QL caused by weak glutes.

This exercise can improve core stability and strengthen the glutes, resulting in improved running mechanics and less stress on your QL. You’ll need a long, looped resistance band.

Industry observers note that sometimes, despite your best at-home efforts to treat an irritated QL, it’s still best to get checked out by a physical therapist. Haas recommends booking a PT appointment if you try the above stretches and strength moves and don’t see improvements after about two weeks.

Industry observers note that agnew suggests getting evaluated by a PT if you’re in so much pain that it’s inhibiting your running. In this case, getting seen sooner can help mitigate pain before further challenges arise, Agnew explains.

Less than 24 hours after his third-place finish at WTCS Abu Dhabi, Hayden Wilde (NZL) showed few outward signs of fatigue as he hit the front of the race in T1, rode among the leaders, and ran his way to victory ahead of training partner Kyle Smith (NZL).

It has been revealed that georgia Taylor-Brown said before the race that she wanted to “beat Julie,” and her wish came true. A small breakaway in the swim put Derron (SUI) on the back foot from the start, while Taylor-Brown had to overcome cramps on the bike and a charging Nicole Van Der Kaay (NZL) on the run to earn a narrow, yet vital victory.

It was a mixed cast of T100 veterans and rookies on the men’s start line, with several notable names absent after the men’s Saudi Arabia T100 race was moved to Dubai on short notice.

Massive news leading into the race was that RaceRanger devices would not be used on the bike due to customs delays in getting the equipment into Dubai, leaving officials to enforce the 20-meter draft zone without the light sensor system.

According to recent reports, A large group emerged from the tepid water to start the bike. After a subpar swim left Wilde chasing in Abu Dhabi the day before, he not only swam with the front group but sprinted through transition, smiling and chatting as he rounded Rico Bogen (GER), showing little sign of the previous day’s effort.

He took his time putting on full-length aero socks as Menno Koolhaas (NED) went straight to the front to lead the men onto the scorching tarmac for 80km of time trialing on the flat course.

The group of 17 after the swim rapidly whittled down to 10 as average speeds approached 30 mph in the opening stages.

According to recent reports, as Bogen, Wilde, and Smith continued to push the pace, the group rapidly dropped to just six. The standout name among the group was Mika Noodt (GER), back racing for the first time since his collision with an ambulance at Ironman 70.3 Swansea in July and already taking turns at the front.

Noodt had been one of the sport’s biggest up-and-coming stars before the accident and was to be Wilde’s strongest challenger on the T100 circuit this year. He has openly shared the mental struggles and trauma that followed the crash, but it seemed he was back to full strength on course as the German powered toward the run.

It has been revealed that off the bike, a quick transition saw Wilde round Bogen for the lead, and he looked set to run away without a challenge. Smith, however, rapidly moved alongside him and stayed there for the opening laps until Wilde turned up the heat.

According to recent reports, from there, there was no stopping him as he put last year’s lap-counting drama in Dubai behind him to head into the Qatar final with a perfect score from his three counting results. Smith held on for his best T100 result of the year, ahead of an emotional Noodt, who marked his return with an immediate trip to the podium.

One of the most remarkable revelations came afterward, when Wilde shared that he believed he had raced much of the day with a broken toe. He injured it during the Aussie exit on the swim and, thinking it might be dislocated, tried to pop it back into place during the bike. Despite the swelling afterward, he mentioned it had not troubled him too much on the run.

A front group of four broke away early on the swim as Taylor-Brown and Kate Waugh’s (GBR) plan to put Derron under pressure from the start worked perfectly. Waugh led through the Aussie exit before Sara Pérez Sala (ESP) led the group into T1.

Derron found herself almost a minute down, but alongside strong riders Caroline Pohle (GER) and Van der Kaay, she remained well within contention. The substantial question was whether her efforts in Kona would affect her race or whether the heat preparation would prove beneficial in the sweltering conditions.

It has been revealed that on the bike, it appeared to be the former as Pohle and Van der Kaay left her behind and worked their way to the front. They eventually helped put more time into Derron, who was over two minutes back and still losing ground on the third lap.

It was not an unfamiliar position for Derron, who had overcome a deficit at the previous women’s race in Vancouver to take down Taylor-Brown and Waugh.

However, it soon became clear that only Taylor-Brown would remain in the fight for the win, with Waugh’s race unraveling in the heat. She later shared on social media that she had started the race sick but still managed to get across the line in ninth, her first T100 finish off the podium.

Everything was going according to plan for Taylor-Brown until she began suffering from adductor cramps late on the bike. She lost positions as she tried to soft-pedal them out, but thankfully for her, they subsided enough for her to start the run just 36 seconds behind Pohle, with Van der Kaay and Pérez Sala also ahead.

Taylor-Brown’s cramps were well in her rearview as she promptly made up the gap and began building a lead. By the third lap, it looked as though that advantage might continue to grow all the way to the finish.

In a recent development, however, Van der Kaay was putting together the best T100 performance of her career and began closing again heading into the final lap. Derron had moved into third but was not making any significant inroads into either athlete ahead.

Van der Kaay put in one final surge to try to catch Taylor-Brown but came up just 10 seconds short. The victory now sends Taylor-Brown into the Grand Final six points clear of Derron and in pole position to become world champion.

Van der Kaay’s excellent performance, which included the second-fastest bike and third-fastest run, moves her into third in the standings heading into the final.

#91742. How to Find Stability and Freedom in Supported Headstand

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2539 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Yogajournal ↗ Open Full Page

How to Find Stability and Freedom in Supported Headstand

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2539 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Yogajournal

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, in Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975.
  • “Sthera sukham asanam,” “Posture is steady and comfortable,” states Patanjali in the first of his three sutras on asana.
  • Industry observers note that because balancing in Headstand (Sirsasana) is such a challenge, it forces us to look deeply into our posture and our nervous system to discover an inner sense of balance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, in Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975. This article about Headstand first appeared in the July-August 1990 matter of Yoga Journal. Find more of our Archives here.

“Sthera sukham asanam,” “Posture is steady and comfortable,” states Patanjali in the first of his three sutras on asana. But as even experienced yoga students know, “steady and comfortable” are not the first words that come to mind to describe the sensation of standing on one’s head. And many couch potatoes would probably insist that they feel quite steady and comfortable as they sprawl out in front of the tube. So what exactly does Patanjali mean by the words sthira and sukham?

Industry observers note that because balancing in Headstand (Sirsasana) is such a challenge, it forces us to look deeply into our posture and our nervous system to discover an inner sense of balance. This interiorization of awareness can reveal some of the subtleties behind Patanjali’s words.

The word thira comes from the Sanskrit root tha, meaning “to stand,” which is also the root of the English words “stay,” “stable,” and “steady.” This root verb is of great importance in the Yoga Sutras. Patanjali first uses it in defining the term abhyasa, or practice, in Sutra I-13: “Practice is the endeavor toward stillness and stability of the mindfield.” According to Pandit Usharbhud Arya’s commentary, “Meditation means bringing the mind to stillness or stability, which means freedom from the rajasic and tamasic turbulences, the mind’s one-pointed concentration on a single sattic vrtti harmonious vibration remaining uninterrupted so that the mind flows in a calm, pacific, smooth stream.”.

Recent findings suggest that for a hatha yoga practitioner, the following question arises: How can I bring this level of mental stillness into an asana such as Headstand, and, conversely, how can I adjust in the asana to stabilize and deepen the mental stillness? In other words, how can I explore the states of thira and sukham in the pose?

In previous asana columns, we have looked at the relationship of the bones, the flesh, and the skin to posture, circulation, and breathing. We have seen that the muscle fibers assist in circulation through their pumping action and that when they are open to the free flow of the breath, they can subtly communicate with the inner lining of the skin. Stability and comfort are accompanied by stable, grounded bones, effortless breathing, a fluid feeling of the flesh, and a sensitive inner skin. Fear, insecurity, and instability, on the other hand, are accompanied by hardened muscles, disturbed breathing, restricted blood flow, collapsed joints, and insensitive skin. The question now becomes: How can I organize the bones, muscle fibers, and skin to create a stable posture that allows the breath and bodily fluids to flow freely?

Industry observers note that freedom or restriction of the breath and bodily fluids can be experienced in the expansion, contraction, and inner pressure of the body’s three main cavities: the pelvic-abdominal cavity (from the diaphragm to the pelvic floor), the thoracic cavity, and the skull. In any posture, the respiratory rhythm begins with an expansion of the thoracic cavity, accomplished by the contraction and descent of the diaphragm and the lifting and widening of the rib cage by the intercostal and other respiratory muscles. This expansion creates a negative pressure (lower than normal atmospheric pres sure) in the chest, drawing air from outside the body into the lungs. With the exhalation, a positive pressure (higher than normal atmospheric pressure) is created as the expansion ceases and the elastic recoil of the lung tissue presses the air out of the lungs.

In soft, quiet breathing, there is no resistance to this cycle. The pelvic-abdominal cavity expands and releases in harmony with the thoracic cavity, and air flows in and out of the body without impedence. The expansion and contraction of the body is perfectly matched by the movement of air in and out of the lungs. Because of this balance, the sensation of interior pressure remains constant throughout the body.

However, any unnecessary tension in the body will create resistance to the breath and a corresponding increase in resistance to the circulatory fluids. This resistance creates the sensation of increased internal pressure, a sensation to which the brain and skull are especially sensitive. To experience this sensation in an exaggerated way, inhale, close your mouth, close your nostrils with your fingers, and try to exhale.

Notice the immediate increase in pressure in the brain. Close your mouth and nostrils after exhaling and you will experience a slightly different pressure increase.

It has been revealed that tension anywhere in the body will have a similar pressurizing effect. For example, neck and shoulder tension restricts the expansion of the rib cage, disrupting the respiratory rhythm and increasing the pressure in the skull. Psychological stresses tend to be reflected in a tense diaphragm, and the diaphragm also reacts to tension in the groins and pelvic region. When the groins are open, the bones of the legs, pelvis, and lower spine support the weight of the body, and the muscles of that region are free to expand and contract with the breathing cycle. However, when the groins are restricted, the pelvic floor cannot.

“breathe,” and this resistance in the pelvic-abdominal region impedes the movement of the diaphragm. This constriction of the breath creates pressure in the skull, just as you experienced when you held your mouth and nostrils shut.

Standing on one’s head exacerbates all of these restrictions to the breath. The shoulders and neck are often tensed to hold on to the body. Fears of falling tighten the diaphragm. The legs and pelvis are often collapsed and unconscious. Thus the breath will be constricted and the brain will feel pressurized. The most obvious aspect of this syndrome is that blood cannot move out of the skull, leading to a sense of congestion. (Some degree of pressure is usual when first starting to practice Headstand; a beginner should not expect to feel perfectly quiet and comfortable right away. But if the eyes become bloodshot or if extreme pressure is felt in the eyes or ears, the pose is being done incorrectly and should not be held. Seek guidance from a qualified teacher.).

The increased pressure in the skull results from a breakdown in the pumping system of the body. The diaphragm is a large pump for moving air, and the skeletal muscles must pump fluids back to the heart to maintain circulation. To facilitate these processes of circulation and respiration, the body is organized into six regions, each with its own “relay station” to oversee the movement of fluids and breath in and out of that region. Although most of these relay stations do not have a single specialized physical component like the diaphragmatic muscle, I will refer to them as diaphragms for lack of a better term, because, like the diaphragm, they function as pumps. (The term “diaphragm” is a convenient metaphor for the complex set of physiological and psychological mechanisms that control the movement of fluids, air, and energy in and out of a particular area of the body.

These diaphragms and their powerful effects can be experienced subjectively by turning the attention inward, although most of them cannot be objectively revealed through dissection.) These diaphragmatic regions, as introduced to me by my teacher, Ramanand Patel, are the brain, the throat, the heart, the respiratory diaphragm, the navel, and the pelvic floor.

In order to attain thira and sukham in Headstand, all six diaphragms must be functioning properly. However, this article will focus on the first and sixth diaphragm, as these are particularly key.

Recent findings suggest that the sixth diaphragm has a tangible physical component, the muscles of the pelvic floor. Open groins, strong legs, and stable hip joints are necessary for the healthy functioning of this diaphragm, which should move synchronously with the physical diaphragm, creating the sense that the pelvis and abdomen breathe freely:.

Sources indicate that correct action of the pelvic diaphragm stabilizes the coccyx bone and helps circulate fluids in and out of the legs. Its location is the first chakra, the chakra of grounding and stability, and thus it plays an important role in developing the quality of shira.

The first diaphragm is the brain or skull diaphragm, responsible for moving energy in the form of blood and cerebrospinal fluid) in and out of the brain. This diaphragm has no muscular components; rather, it is composed of a complex combination of neural pathways and blood vessels. My experience has been that it moves in opposition to the other five diaphragms: When the other five diaphragms are “inhaling,” or drawing energy in, the brain diaphragm is “exhaling,” or releasing. Conversely, when the lower five are exhaling, the brain “inhales.” This is the rhythm that accompanies a healthy nervous and circulatory system, leading to shira and sukham.

It has been revealed that however, if the pelvic diaphragm is locked or inhibited, the brain diaphragm will “inhale” along with the torso, leading to an increase in tension in the muscles and pressure in the skull. This tension can also be felt as disturbances in the skin, eyes, ears, and tongue.

Recent findings suggest that before attempting Headstand, you should have a strong, stable Downward-Facing Dog Pose and a regular standing pose practice to ensure the strength, flexibility, and intelligence of your arms and legs necessary to protect the neck and skull. Use a firm blanket or mat for the head. If possible, learn to balance in a corner of the room, resting one foot on each wall to prevent tilting to one side or another. If a corner is not available, use any wall, placing your hands close to the wall to keep from arching your back into a banana shape.

Place your forearms on the floor, interlocking your fingers evenly and completely and keeping your wrists perpendicular to the floor. Your elbows should be exactly shoulder width apart. This foundation must be stabilized by constant practice.

In building this foundation, several difficulties may be encountered. One arm may overpower the other, distorting the shoulders, forearms, and wrists and torquing the foundation. Learn to press evenly into both arms. Your wrists may collapse outward, losing their grounding and strength. Consciously hold the thumb side of your wrists toward each other. Your elbows may splay apart. Maintain a constant pressure from your outer elbows toward each other, as if your elbows were pressing into a block held between them. However, do not draw them closer than shoulder width.

Having established this stable foundation, place your head up against your wrists and palms, cupping your skull without losing the strength of the wrists. Taking the weight onto the arms and not the neck, use the strength of the groins and pelvis to lift both legs up from the floor. (Beginners will probably have to throw one leg up at a time, but as soon as possible should begin lifting both at once.) Resting your feet against the wall, lift the weight of the body out of the shoulders, away from the neck.

According to recent reports, learning this lifting action is more important than learning to balance. Only when the lift is strong and the balance stable should you move to the center of the room.

Students who can balance steadily in the center of the room can begin to explore the effect on the pose of the pelvic and brain diaphragms. Most beginning students look something like the “inverted banana” in Figure 1. Your shoulders sink, the floating ribs and upper lumbar hang forward, your back body collapses, and your legs fall behind the midline. With no vertical extension, the weight of the torso collapses onto your neck and skull, compressing the brain diaphragm. The legs are not lifting, and their weight hardens the posterior pelvic floor and the inner front groins. The anterior coccyx bone hangs unsupported.

Instead, your arms and shoulders must lift actively away from the neck and skull. Figure 2 shows a close-up of the correct lifting action. Note the widening of the upper inner shoulder blades and the lifting of the inner and outer deltoid muscles, which lifts the weight of the torso away from the neck and skull. This action can be learned in Downward-Facing Dog (Adho Mukha Svanasana).

Your legs also must be brought forward, lifting the lumbar, pelvis, and legs to eliminate the banana-like collapse. Intermediate students often learn this action, only to close the anterior pelvis and inner groins and lose the support of the posterior coccyx (see Figure 3). The front and inner groins must be dynamically extended, without collapsing onto the lumbar. Your legs must work tremendously in Headstand to open the pelvic diaphragm. In working the legs, be sure to extend the bones from the pelvis without hardening and tensing the muscles—rather, keep the muscles vibrant. If the leg muscles harden, the pelvic diaphragm will tighten and the brain will become pressurized and confused.

Recent findings suggest that in the completed position (Figure 5), your front body and back body extend evenly, aligning the bones with gravity. When the bones are aligned, they can support the weight of the body without muscular strain. Figure 4 has been inverted to show the alignment of the arches, knees, hips, shoulders, and ears. By lifting evenly out of the pelvis, the bones of the legs free the pelvic diaphragm to breathe and pump blood to the legs. The dynamic action of the legs lifts the weight of the torso from the skull, allowing the brain diaphragm to breathe.

In a recent development, the anterior and posterior sides of the coccyx bone are supported, freeing the pelvic diaphragm. This freedom allows the respiratory diaphragm to breathe easily, which in turn allows the brain to feel relaxed and spacious. Thus the whole pose feels spacious, stable, and comfortable.

Stability and comfort are prerequisites for deeper work in the poses. As Vyassa states in his commentary to the first of the Yoga Sutras, yoga is samadhi. Sthira and sukham are the beginning of the samadhi state and thus are the point at which true yoga commences. All previous action is preparatory in nature. To achieve thira and sukham, it is not sufficient just to sit in any comfortable pose. Rather, you must perfect the pose to such an extent that samadhi can spontaneously awaken.

Sources indicate that the universe is alive, awakening and creating itself anew with each moment. If we create the proper foundations of shira and sukham, so that our mind and body are clear and calm, we can directly experience this awakening and creativity. With 10 years until the turn of the millenium, human consciousness is awakening to its own inner potentials as it is simultaneously awakening to the potentials of the natural world. All serious practitioners of yoga should work to be stabilized at least in the beginning level of thira and sukham by then, so we can usher in a newly introduced age of planetary awakening, with wisdom, compassion, and ecological communion with the natural world as our goals.

Here’s What to Know About the Nike Vaporfly 5

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (882 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article.
  • Nike announced a whole slate of innovations it has in the works, including a new method for creating Air units, the return of the Nike Free, and a look at the future of its sportswear.
  • Recent findings suggest that the massive highlight is that the road racing shoe is basically going to have a “spring” in it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Nike announced a whole slate of innovations it has in the works, including a new method for creating Air units, the return of the Nike Free, and a look at the future of its sportswear. But the most interesting product unveiling is the Vaporfly 5—Nike is calling it the “most aggressive Vaporfly yet.”.

Recent findings suggest that the massive highlight is that the road racing shoe is basically going to have a “spring” in it. “At the center of Vaporfly 5 is a newly introduced, wave-shaped Flyplate,” Nike’s announcement read. “A ripple through the midfoot creates a spring-like sensation under the arch.”.

I got a look at the prototype in Chicago last month, when I visited Nike’s headquarters during marathon weekend. There, I asked Bret Schoolmeester, vice president of running footwear product, if he was concerned about calling the shoe a spring. He is not, and told me that shoes basically serve as springs already given the bouncy modern foams being used.

Sources indicate that remember back to the first carbon-plated shoes, when much of the uproar around them was because people believed the plates would act like springs. That’s not really what came to fruition, as we found that the plates basically were used as stiffening mechanisms to create leverage.

According to recent reports, world Athletics rules permit a plate in a single layer, and that’s what Nike is technically creating here. The difference is in the shaping. The bump in this newly introduced plate, combined with the midsole geometry, will allow the plate to flex when you land and snap back to shape to propel you ahead.

Industry observers note that nike also looked at ways to strip weight, which you can see through the big carve-outs in the foam, the super thin Vapor Mesh upper, and sparse use of Goatek outsole. Another weight-saving measure is adding ZoomX LT, the lightweight version of ZoomX that we saw in the Alphafly 4. A thin layer of that sits between the plate and your foot, while the standard ZoomX is used between the plate and the road for control and responsiveness.

Industry observers note that with these changes, Nike is positioning this shoe to be a shorter-distance road racing shoe. Given the overhaul of the Alphafly 4 and the announcement of the Apex, a hyper shoe designed for elite marathoners, the Vaporfly is being pitched for races up to 13.1 miles. Sure, some runners will lace it up for a full marathon, though it’s going to be lighter and snappier to excel at faster speeds.

The shoe won’t be available until “fall 2027,” but Nike is showing it off early as it drums up excitement for upcoming footwear and apparel at its World of Athletes event.

Beyond the Vaporfly 5, there were some other cool new innovations announced, including “Tuned Air.” Through a new manufacturing process, Nike is able to create lighter Air units more quickly, which can be customized for various applications.

I spoke with Phil McCartney, executive vice president, chief innovation, design and product officer, last week about Tuned Air. He explained that through a proprietary digital print and selective lamination process, Air units can be created with different amounts of cushioning and support. Those characteristics are delivered not only through the physical geometries of the Air unit, but also by varying the pressure within each unit.

Nike has previously talked about “Tuned Air,” and we saw it in use with the Pegasus Plus 2. But that was really just offering a few different air bags. The idea is that bigger shoes are worn by bigger runners and, thus, bigger Air units with greater gas pressures are required. So, shoes any smaller than a women’s 7.5 (M6) got an Air unit that’s 9.5 mm thick with 15 psi. Moving on up to a men’s 10.5 (W12), the bag gains 2 mm thickness. And, those runners with larger feet sit atop the 11.5mm-thick unit pumped up with 20 psi.

These newly introduced units, however, are different altogether. Nike found a way to remove the need for pins and rigid zones that formed the Air units, so that each can offer better cushioning and responsiveness.

Industry observers note that like the Vaporfly 5, Tuned Air won’t make an appearance until later in 2027. The prototype shoe teased in the image above has one massive Air unit making up the entire midsole. No word yet on which model or franchise that shoe will reside.

While we wait, the fastest Nike available to any of us remains the Alphafly 4.

Jeff is Runner-in-Chief for Runner’s World and the director of product testing. He has tested and reviewed running shoes, GPS watches, headphones, apparel, and more for nearly two decades. He regularly tests more than 100 pairs of shoes each year, and once had a 257-day streak running in different models. Jeff can usually be found on the roads, racing anything from the mile to a marathon, but he also enjoys racing up mountains and on snowshoes. When he’s not running, you’ll probably find him hanging from a ladder making repairs and renovations to his house (he’s also director of product testing for Popular Mechanics).

The 15 percent incline and 3 percent decline range means you’re getting real terrain simulation, and the generous belt gives even tall runners room to fully open their stride.

Sources indicate that the 24-inch touchscreen tilts and swivels, and with iFit, you can chase coaches through mountain trails or city streets. They have basically a gajillion classes, programs, and virtual runs that keep things interesting.

At $2,299, it’s not for casual people, but it’s great for people planning to log serious miles. We are those people. Years in, it still earns its spot. Grab it while the holiday weekend deal is active and don’t look back.

This treadmill is a workhorse. I have friends and acquaintances who have had one of these in their home for years and years and still haven’t had them serviced. Do I recommend that? Absolutely not, but it is a testament to the strength and durability of this treadmill. It’s built to hop on and go, though you can scroll through several programs, or hook it up to your smartphone app and access it through the 10-inch touchscreen.

Sources indicate that it has a 15 percent incline potential, which is wonderful for those families who have a runner and someone who likes to do incline walking or weighted walks indoors. Personally, I love the oversized belt, comfortable running surface, and the simple controls that don’t have you accidentally going from 0 to 12 miles per hour because you hit the roller by accident when you were reaching for your water bottle.

According to recent reports, this is WalkingPad’s entrant into the traditional treadmill space, doing what they do best—making an easy-to-store treadmill that delivers on its promises. At more than 50 inches long and 20 inches wide, this is their largest treadmill. Unlike their other machines, this bad boy can reach up to 11.5 miles per hour, which is way faster than I run; I can tell you that much.

And perhaps the best part? It folds up small enough to hide behind your sofa or in your closet, thanks to WalkingPad’s ingenious double fold that lets you fold the treadmill deck in half and into itself. It’s a genuinely wild thing to see, and I’m excited.

If you’re 5-foot-10 or under and pressed for space, this might be your best deal yet. It’s a fully folding, 20-by-53-inch deck ‘mill with 15 percent incline, easy operations, and the best thing? You’re not locked into one system. You can hook up Peloton, Zwift, or iFit, and you’re set. If you aren’t interested in that, you get hundreds of workouts on the Sunny Health app for free. It’s a solid treadmill at a reasonable price.

According to recent reports, cat Bowen, senior editor of commerce; reviews, is a seasoned runner with more than 20 years of distance running experience, including dozens of marathons, half marathons, and even a few ultra marathons. For over a decade, she has tested parenting, fitness, home, and running gear and written in-depth guides to help readers with their next purchase. Holding multiple advanced degrees and presently studying kinesiology, Cat Bowen brings research-backed insight to all of her guides. Passionate about women’s health and neurodivergent inclusion, she advocates for closing research gaps and helping others—especially AudHD people—find joy in running and fitness.

#91737. What’s the Minimum Amount of Mileage You Can Do to Maintain Fitness? Experts Answer

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1359 w)
📖 Baca

What’s the Minimum Amount of Mileage You Can Do to Maintain Fitness? Experts Answer

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1359 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For some runners, taking a week or two off from running after a race is the hard part—they can’t wait to ramp back up their volume again.
  • Industry observers note that still, if you trained for months to build up the fitness, including your aerobic capacity, lactate threshold, and running economy, you probably want to try to maintain at least some of that afterward.
  • Maintenance mode also gives you the flexibility to be able to jump into a 10K or half-marathon on a whim, claims Mike Sheehy, running coach for Team Abbott who has completed more than 100 marathons.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For some runners, taking a week or two off from running after a race is the hard part—they can’t wait to ramp back up their volume again. But for others, crossing a finish line (of any distance) might feel like a natural point to take a break from the sport, or at least to significantly scale back.

Industry observers note that still, if you trained for months to build up the fitness, including your aerobic capacity, lactate threshold, and running economy, you probably want to try to maintain at least some of that afterward. That way, you can go into a spring training cycle with a solid base.

Maintenance mode also gives you the flexibility to be able to jump into a 10K or half-marathon on a whim, claims Mike Sheehy, running coach for Team Abbott who has completed more than 100 marathons.

Keeping a steady mileage base also allows you to experiment. “This gives you a chance to try newly introduced fuels, try new gear, a new pair of shorts, new pair of shoes, stuff you didn't like during your block,” Sheehy says. You could also experiment with pace. “This is a great block to think about moving your easy pace up 15 seconds to let your heart and body start adapting to that new norm.”.

Recent findings suggest that if you want to strike a balance between giving yourself a well-deserved break and completely reversing all of your gains, the question becomes: What’s the minimum running you can do to maintain your fitness? And how long can I do that without falling back?

Here’s what running coaches and an exercise physiologist have to say, plus what other forms of exercise come into play in the maintenance phase.

GET YOUR MAINTENANCE PLANS HERE.

First, it’s important to note that taking a week or two off after a marathon and at least one week for the half is not only encouraged, it’s probably the best thing you can do for your body—and your mind.

“The thing I encourage all my runners to remember is patience,” claims Sheehy. “Let your body heal and take that time.” He typically advises runners to take a full week off, then slowly add in easy miles without rushing to get back to quality workouts.

Recent findings suggest that then by the end of week two, you enter the true maintenance phase. “This is really an exciting time of running,” Sheehy notes. “This is where we’re keeping 90 percent of the fitness with about 60 percent of the work.” He recommends taking the average mileage from your peak marathon training weeks rather than the single highest weekly mileage.

This tends to net out to between 20 and 30 miles a week in the maintenance phase for marathon runners and 10 to 15 miles a week for half-marathoners. That might look like three shorter, easier runs during the week and an 8- to 12-miler on the weekend. (Experts agree it’s best to run more frequently at lower volume for each run than do fewer, longer runs.) “That keeps you 90 percent fit, but allows you to enjoy running and not have the pressure of having to run six or five days a week and without having structured workouts,” Sheehy says.

Andrew M. Jones, Ph.D., professor of applied physiology at the University of Exeter in the U.K., puts the minimum effective dose of maintenance running slightly lower—at 50 percent—though after about four to six weeks at half the volume, runners will likely start to see “more significant deterioration,” he states, specifically of race-specific endurance. (Running economy may be more resilient.).

That’s not necessarily a bad thing (and allows you to focus on other goals; more on this soon), and 50 percent is enough to preserve a foundation to allow you to pick up at the beginning of a 16-week marathon training proposal with relative ease.

Greg Laraia, a running coach at Motiv in Upcoming York City, agrees and provides this example: Say a runner finished Berlin on September 27 and intends to run London on April 24. After time off, he’d have them work back up to 50 percent of their mileage by October 25, then hover in the 50 to 60 percent of mileage range until early January when their London block would start in earnest.

Sources indicate that retaining intensity during the maintenance phase is arguably more notable than frequency and duration, per Jones. “It’s impossible to give a minimum effective dose [for intensity] but ideally by week two [after a marathon] they’d get back to the pre-marathon training intensity but with lower volume,” he notes, which might be lower duration and/or frequency of quality running. “Intensity is the key stimulus.”.

To hit this stimulus, Sheehy and Laraia both like to have runners add in strides (e.g., four to six 30- to 60-second strides as part of an easy run) before doing more intense speed workouts that could make their way back into the weekly schedule about a month after a race.

Sheehy provides an example of a speed workout he likes to include during the maintenance phase:.

According to recent reports, “The upcoming race pace is something I know they can achieve that is apparent in previous race results and workouts; not some aspirational wish pace,” Sheehy notes. “This will give them the confidence they need or maybe a wake up call, but it makes for a great starting point, and allows us to calibrate their easy paces and use the lower volumes to let their body (and heart) adjust to the new norm.”.

Sheehy cautions against swapping out runs that make up your maintenance mileage for other cardio, as it is notable to maintain the specificity of running if you want to maintain running fitness. But he often adds in an indoor cycling day during his offseason on top of four or so days of running. If you dropped down your running frequency, an aerobic cross-training workout can support your fitness maintenance. Plus, it gives you a mental break, Jones says.

According to recent reports, laraia indicates one case where swapping maintenance miles for other cardio could make sense would be when runners come off a fall race injured or worn down and simply need a break from running so much. “Running is always going to be the best option because running is the sport, but if an elliptical or a bike is going to make you miss [running] enough to want to do it again, let’s start there,” he says.

Industry observers note that the maintenance phase is also a great time to focus on strength training, Jones says. Sheehy agrees, suggesting aiming for two to three days a week. You can do more volume (either via an extra day or more sets/reps) during this phase, but it’s still notable to include one true rest day in your plan, Sheehy says.

Strength work helps to build neuromuscular capacity, improve power that can translate to speed, and strengthen your tendons and ligaments for the upcoming season, especially if you focus on heavier lifting. “Let’s get comfortable with the extra load and then let’s see if it makes running better and more efficient,” Laraia says.

GET YOUR STRENGTH WORKOUTS HERE.

Laraia says signs that you may have pulled back too much include a higher-than-usual heart rate during runs or paces that feel harder than normal.

Sources indicate that still, it’s probably better to lose a little bit more running fitness in the offseason than to push yourself too hard, he states. The former is going to put you in a better position to start a new training block in the spring, compared with the latter, which could lead to burnout and could set your next training cycle back.

“Realistically, you’re going to be better off taking the extra day versus trying to push through something if you’re early in a block or just trying to maintain fitness,” Laraia states. “I’d rather you be 100 percent recovered for every run versus in the build,” where it might make sense to go into a run feeling a little depleted.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Fall riding season is coming to a close, and winter is right around the corner. While late fall and winter mean shorter daylight hours for riding, it’s a great time to save on cycling gear—for yourself or if shopping early for holiday gifts. Many brands are discounting old inventory at great prices, and others are clearing room for new gear hitting shelves after the New Year.

It has been revealed that although many of the best holiday sales aren’t until Black Friday and Cyber Monday, some retailers are running Early Black Friday promotions with substantial deals and discounts on top-rated gear. In addition to Pre-Black Friday sales, Amazon, REI, bike brands, and other retailers are offering deep discounts on cycling equipment, components, apparel, and accessories you need for road, gravel, and mountain bike rides.

It has been revealed that pre-Black Friday sales are a great chance to stock up on frequently used consumables—such as tubes, tire sealant, chain lube, and nutrition products—and to grab the gear you need for late-fall and winter rides. They’re also a great way to save money on usually pricey riding apparel: If you’ve been holding out on buying a upcoming vest, arm warmers, jerseys, a jacket, or even shoes, some brands are offering deep discounts on cycling clothing and accessories.

Below are sales and deals hubs for several top online cycling gear and bike retailers, plus links to sales from leading clothing brands and bike companies. These are some of the best deals on editor-tested gear we’ve spotted so far. Bookmark this page and return for updates as even more deals come online.

➜ AMAZON ➜ REI ➜ BACKCOUNTRY ➜ COMPETITIVE CYCLIST ➜ BIKE TIRES DIRECT ➜ PEARL IZUMI ➜ VELOCIO ➜ CAPO ➜ ORNOT ➜ WAHOO ➜ ZWIFT ➜ SPECIALIZED ➜ TREK.

Bike lights are a must-have item for anyone commuting or riding road or gravel in the winter months. Even if you already have a light, I’ve found it super useful to own an extra set to have at the office, on my other bikes, or as spares for friends.

Lezyne consistently makes great front and rear lights. While slightly pricier than budget picks found on Amazon or AliExpress, they’re durable, work well, and last several seasons. Plus, we’ve found Lezyne’s advertised runtimes and lumens are much closer to reality than many no-name lights.

Industry observers note that showers Pass makes our best-tested winter gloves, and they’re presently on sale at 19% off. In their review, our test rider said, “This knit, waterproof glove has a midweight feel and sufficient insulation when temperatures hover around freezing. Most riders will find the Crosspoints reach its limit at about 30-35 degrees, depending on how hard you’re riding.”.

The glove traps some body heat, so your fingers may be slightly chilly at first but will warm up within 15 minutes. Better yet, when the mercury climbs, your hands won’t feel hot and sweaty.

It has been revealed that electric mini-inflators burst onto the scene a couple of years ago and have swiftly become a rider favorite for pumping up your tires at home, at the trailhead, or on rides. Of the inflators we’ve tested, the RockBros model stands out for its consistency and is a favorite of Bicycling editors. It’s compact, lightweight, and has an accurate gauge. In our testing of 15 electric pumps, it inflated a road tire to 65 psi in 45 seconds, and filled five tires before running out of power.

The Wahoo Kickr Core 2—Bicycling’s Best Overall Indoor Trainer—is on sale for the lowest price we’ve seen: $399.99. The Core combines excellent performance, great accuracy, and high max resistance in a package perfect for Zwift rides after work, winter training, and even competitive virtual racing.

It has been revealed that indoor training bikes are rapidly gaining popularity for their ease of use and low maintenance. With a dedicated indoor setup, you no longer have to wrestle with getting your bike on or off the smart trainer, which also makes it convenient to share with other riders in your family. Plus, you won’t wear out pricey parts. Zwift’s Ride is our favorite: it sets up quickly and adjusts for a wide range of rider heights and fits. It also costs thousands less than its competitors.

It has been revealed that shorter daylight hours and lower temps often mean fewer hours spent riding outside on the road or trail. An indoor trainer helps you maintain your fitness through the winter months while getting your riding fix. Garmin’s Tacx Flux2 is the brand’s mid-range smart trainer; with 2,000 watts of resistance, it simulates gradients up to 16%. The Flux also connects to virtual platforms like Zwift and Rouvy for immersive indoor riding experiences.

Industry observers note that stainless bottles have become popular among cyclists over the past several seasons. They keep water chilled on hot rides and don’t give your water a funny plastic taste. Many gravel and off-road riders love CamelBak’s Stainless Podium, particularly for its open/closed twist-lock cap. The Podium Stainless also ranked best in our heat testing last summer and performed well in our winter bottle testing.

SUMMER BOTTLE TESTING WINTER BOTTLE TESTING.

Industry observers note that elite road and gravel helmets offer low weight, excellent ventilation, and great looks. However, those benefits usually come at a high cost. Giro’s Agilis Mips helmet is a great option if you want a pro-level look and performance without the associated price.

Weighing 299 grams (size medium), my Agilis is only 15 grams heavier than Giro’s premium Aries Spherical model—and the Agilis costs significantly less. The Agilis is very well-ventilated, comparable to the priciest lids on all but the hottest of rides.

Recent findings suggest that this helmet features Mips technology to protect your brain from rotational forces in a crash, and Giro’s Hardbody co-molded shell to better protect it from small bumps and dings when not on your head. Plus, the Agilis uses the Roc-Loc dial system to ensure a proper fit.

Recent findings suggest that MET’s Trenta 3K Carbon is one of the top five road helmets by Virginia Tech’s helmet lab. It’s also one of the best for racing and high-performance riding, as proven by UAE Team Emirates’s results—Tour de France champion Tadej Pogačar and World Champion Brandon McNulty. While UAE riders often race the Italian brand’s Manta aero helmet, they pick the lightweight, well-ventilated Trenta 3K Carbon for climbing stages and training.

Industry observers note that unlike some modern helmets with similarly strong protection, the Trenta feels light and racey on your head, and almost disappears when you’re riding. The straps offer good adjustability, and the Mips Air Node liner protects without feeling bulky. However, the Trenta’s biggest drawback is its price tag. Typically priced over $500, this is an expensive piece of kit, but this deal cuts the cost by almost a third.

Arm warmers are among the most versatile pieces of cycling clothing you can own. This magical piece of kit turns your short-sleeve jersey into a long-sleeve in seconds—and you can change back to short sleeves again mid-ride if the temps rise.

In a recent development, I’ve owned many pairs of arm warmers over the last three decades, and I rarely ride without them on my arms or in my jersey pocket if the temperatures are between 45 and 60 degrees. Castelli makes some of the best clothes out there, and these arm warmers are a steal for the price. They’re easy to pull on or off while riding, and they don’t sag.

A quality rain jacket is a must-have item for riders who live anywhere it rains or snows. Rapha’s Core Rain Jacket is great option for layering over your winter jersey without adding too much bulk. It features a two-way zip for regulating body temperature, reflective hits for riding after dusk or in the early morning, and packs down small if weather clears mid-ride.

Industry observers note that if you ride in temps below 40 degrees, a good cycling jacket is a great asset. As a Scottish brand, Endura knows a few things about riding in the cold, dark days of winter, and its MT500 Freezing Point jacket is a great option for trail rides and commuting in low temps. It features PrimaLoft Gold insulation and a DWR finish to shed rain drops. Another great feature is the MT500’s underarm zippers; they allow you to cool off and ventilate without unzipping your entire jacket.

When cold weather hits, bib tights ensure you stay warm on rides. Of the many cycling tights available, Velocio makes some of our test editors’ favorites. The One Thermal bibs feature a soft, fleece lining and use a more relaxed, less compressive fit than some of the brands’ other options. This makes them perfect for road, gravel, and trail rides, or even layering under commuter pants.

Recent findings suggest that instead of shredding your nice, lightweight road tires on weather-worn winter roads, swap them out for more durable rubber. Vittoria’s Rubino tires are a proven all-season road tire with a smooth, fast-rolling center and siped edges for cornering traction. They’re tubeless-compatible, so you’ll catch fewer flats in the cold, and come in widths from 26mm to 34mm with black or tan sidewalls.

Modern bike computers do much more than display speed and distance. These devices are a critical information hub for many cyclists. Cycling computers can record ride metrics, display real-time performance data, and help you navigate—but that’s only scratching the surface of their capabilities.

It has been revealed that the Elemnt Bolt 3 is Wahoo’s tiny-but-mighty cycling-specific computer. Wahoo equips it with a 2.3-inch high-resolution screen, up to 20 hours of battery life, and integration with Strava, Komoot, and other popular cycling platforms.

It has been revealed that another great option is the Hammerhead Karoo. This head unit features a 3.2-inch color touchscreen Gorilla Glass display and up to 35 hours of run time. The Karoo stands out for its mapping and navigation. The navigation, combined with its pop-up hill climb feature and ability to sideload apps, makes the Karoo my overall favorite.

Recent findings suggest that POC makes comfortable, well-ventilated helmets for road, gravel, and mountain biking. The Kortal is a trail-style helmet, featuring an adjustable visor, room to stow your glasses or goggles, and plenty of airflow for hot summer trail rides. The straps are also comfortable, something that often bugs me on other lids.

In a recent development, fresh bar tape is the quickest and most cost-effective way to improve the look, feel, and comfort of any road or gravel bike. I’ve used Fizik tape on several bikes that have come in for testing, and have also bought it for my personal bikes. It has enough cushion, reliable grip, and is easy to wrap. You can’t ask for much more from bar tape.

While many riders are adding electric mini-inflators to their tool kits, a quality floor pump remains an essential part of every cyclist’s arsenal. They never run out of batteries, pump as many tires as your arms can handle, and are easy to use.

Riders and mechanics have trusted Topeak’s JoeBlow pumps for decades—because they work. Although many JoeBlow models are low-cost and utilitarian, the JoeBlow Ace DX is a Cadillac-level floor pump. It features alloy construction with a metal chuck and can inflate tires up to 260 psi, with three different inflation modes: high-volume, standard, or high-pressure.
