#91722. Best Winter Cycling Gloves for Cold, Wet, and Windy Rides

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1818 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Bicycling ↗ Open Full Page

Best Winter Cycling Gloves for Cold, Wet, and Windy Rides

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1818 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Sources indicate that nothing ruins a chilly, crisp day on the bike faster than frozen fingers.
  • The right pair of winter gloves will keep your hands warm without making it difficult to operate your bike’s controls.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Sources indicate that nothing ruins a chilly, crisp day on the bike faster than frozen fingers. Besides being uncomfortable, numb hands can make it difficult to shift gears or feel your brake levers, turning a cold ride into a potentially unsafe one.

The right pair of winter gloves will keep your hands warm without making it difficult to operate your bike’s controls. But finding that pair isn’t always as simple as checking the temperature rating on the packaging. How warm your hands get, the weather conditions, and the type of riding you do all play a role.

For example, on a 35-degree road ride, you’ll likely want a much warmer glove than you would for a mountain bike ride at the same temperature. Higher speeds on the road mean more windchill, while a slower, harder effort on the trails can leave your hands sweaty in gloves that are too warm. If you ride throughout the winter, it’s worth owning a few different pairs to cover the range of conditions you’ll encounter.

I tested more than 40 glove models in temperatures ranging from the low 60s to below 20 degrees, then narrowed the field to my six favorites. I’ve included recommended temperature ranges for each, but consider those a starting point. If you tend to run cold or have Raynaud’s syndrome, you may want a warmer glove; if your hands sweat easily, a lighter, more breathable option might work better.

Sources indicate that more Winter Gear Advice: Our Expert Swears by This Three-Layer Trick. ● The Best Men’s Winter Cycling Jackets ● The Best Winter Cycling Hats.

Perhaps my all-time favorite version of my all-time favorite glove, DeFeet’s Duraglove has been around for ages and has remained mostly unchanged. It’s very comfortable, has great dexterity, and provides good grip. Plus, it has touchscreen functionality. DeFeet offers two versions of this glove: The plain Duraglove ET and the Duraglove ET Wool Blend featured here, which uses a merino wool blend.

It has been revealed that I’ve found this version to be the warmer of the two. I’ve worn this glove into the low 40s during high-intensity rides and stayed comfortable. Because this knit glove is incredibly breathable, it’s still comfortable to wear as the day warms into the mid-to-high 50s. The Duraglove is unsuitable for rainy rides as its knit construction will swiftly soak up water.

These Assos gloves feel like they shouldn’t be as warm as they are. But don’t let their thin, stretchy, low-bulk material fool you. These gloves have kept my hands toasty and comfortable into the high 30s, and I have mountain biked in them at near-freezing temperatures with no issues.

They use soft fleece fabric inside and have an outer layer with excellent wind resistance. Assos also applies a water-repellent treatment to manage light rain and spray from damp roads. I’m a major fan of the palm of these gloves. They feature very minimal padding that helps with grip and bar feel. Fit and construction are excellent, with long cuffs to keep cold air out of your jacket, plus touchscreen functionality that works very well. The only knock against these gloves is their price. However, my personal pair is now in its fourth winter with no signs of wear, making these an easy recommendation if you want a good pair of gloves that will last.

Sources indicate that near-freezing temperatures with rain are probably the most challenging conditions to ride in. But for some, it’s unavoidable. Glacier Glove’s Ice Bay is as good as it gets for these conditions. It’s constructed with 2mm-thick, fleece-lined neoprene and is as waterproof as any piece of clothing could be.

These gloves have incredible dexterity given their warmth. The long cuff is easy to tuck under your rain jacket to keep water out. The downside of a neoprene glove is that it does not breathe at all. That’s partly how it keeps your hands warm, but it only works as long as you keep the gloves on. If you take them off, your now-sweaty hands will get quite cold promptly, and your formerly toasty gloves (lacking body heat) will be cold and wet with sweat. Despite these drawbacks, if it’s cold and rainy and I need to be out riding, these are the gloves I reach for.

Recent findings suggest that these pricey gloves are the warmest five-finger gloves I’ve tried that still let me move my fingers. Gore took inspiration from high alpine mountaineering for the design. The outer shell uses a Gore-Tex ePE liner that is highly wind- and water-resistant. For insulation, Gore used a PrimaLoft lining. It features one of the best warmth-to-weight ratios. All of this results in a glove that can be comfortable down to and below freezing, depending on your pace and specific riding conditions.

Sources indicate that I’ve used similarly warm gloves from other brands, and they've often been far too bulky to feel useful. These still maintain a good bar feel and let me freely articulate my fingers. While they have touchscreen compatibility, I found them a little too bulky to quickly type out a text message on an iPhone.

We’ve been using Pearl Izumi’s AmFIB Lobster Gloves for more than a decade. And they’re still one of the best gloves for when temps plummet.

In a recent development, the gloves are made with 170g PrimaLoft Gold insulation, AmFIB soft-shell polyester-polyurethane fabric, and Ax Suede Laredo synthetic leather. It has the kind of exceptional warmth you’d get in a mitten. Yet the AmFIBs still allow for ample dexterity so you can operate both your shifters and brake levers. There’s also a gel palm pad for comfort while gripping the handlebar, plus touchscreen compatibility for the index finger and thumb.

In a recent development, the secret to the dexterity is the PrimaLoft Gold insulation, which provides exceptional warmth without adding bulk. Most very warm gloves are also very thick, which makes it difficult to locate the proper shifter and grip your brake levers. This pair keeps my hands warm on long weekend rides and daily commutes, even when temperatures dip below freezing, without getting in the way.

Industry observers note that bar Mitts may look unconventional, but riders who use them swear by their added warmth and control. Designed to work with gloves, these neoprene covers attach to your bar and enclose your bike’s shifters and brake levers. They add significant wind protection and help keep your hands shielded from the elements.

It has been revealed that several Bar Mitt variants are available for road, mountain, and townie-style handlebars. Be sure to check details and confirm fitment with your bar/shifter combo before you order.

Glove fit is subjective. They should fit in the Goldilocks range. If your gloves are too big, you risk losing grip on the handlebar and controls. But a glove that’s too tight can prevent you from comfortably grasping the handlebar or grips.

It has been revealed that an easy way to spot a glove that’s too big is if you have a lot of fabric bunching in your palm. It’s always worth trying new gloves on your bike to see how they feel on the bars, since labeled sizing can differ from brand to brand.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re riding in temperatures below the mid-40s or closer to freezing, you want a glove with some insulation. In the most basic definition, insulation is filling used to capture and hold onto warmth. The most familiar insulation for outdoor use is down, often found in puffy jackets. In gloves, you are most likely to find down in very bulky mittens, which are very warm but lack the dexterity for cycling.

In a recent development, most cycling-specific gloves use synthetic insulation from companies like Polartech or PrimaLoft. These materials are most often used on the back of the hand to protect from wind and minimize interference with the handlebar feel. Thin, grippy material is generally found on the palm. Many brands use leather on the palms for improved grip and durability, so watch out for this if you avoid buying animal products.

According to recent reports, for the interior of the glove, look for polyester or Merino wool. You want something that wicks sweat and keeps your hands dry—sweaty hands can rapidly turn into frozen prunes.

According to recent reports, gloves with appropriate breathability for the temperature and your riding effort keep your hands warm and dry. The warmer the temps, or the higher your effort, the more breathable you’ll want your gloves.

Regionally, humidity also plays a part in selecting the right glove. If you ride somewhere cool and dry, such as Colorado, where it might be in the 30s with low humidity, you likely will be able to use a lighter pair of more breathable gloves. These can do a much better job keeping you warm because they transfer moisture away from your hands more effectively. If you ride in the Northeast, the same pair of gloves might feel too cold at the same temperature, since humidity is often much higher. For these conditions, you’ll want a glove with better wind and waterproofing at the expense of breathability.

Sources indicate that once you figure out the glove warmth you need for your riding, consider other features before buying. Something I find very notable in gloves meant for frigid weather is long cuffs. Cuffs make it easy to tuck the glove under or sometimes over your jacket sleeve, keeping your wrists warm and stopping cold air from entering your jacket.

In a recent development, the palm construction of a glove is also worth careful examination. A common feature is padding. Some riders prefer padded gloves, while others do not. Padding matters less the warmer a glove gets, since the palm becomes bulkier with insulation. For thinner gloves, a seamless palm is the way to go. It minimizes any chance of irritation and improves handlebar feel.

If you ride with a smartphone or have a touchscreen computer, gloves that interact with these devices are great. The less you need to remove your gloves in the cold, the happier your hands will be.

Finally, a soft, large terrycloth nose-wipe section (preferably along the thumb or index finger) is good if you’re a heavy snotter.

Prior to joining Bicycling in 2021, Dan worked as part of the race organization for the Red Hook Crit, as a coach with EnduranceWERX, as well as a freelance writer and photographer.

Fashion Has Entered Its Running Era

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (741 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article.
  • According to recent reports, there was a time when you could spot someone who had just finished a run.
  • Running shoes have officially entered their fashion era, and while the whole sneaker-meets-streetwear thing isn't exactly newly introduced (the chunky dad sneaker era still lives rent-free in my head), the latest wave of collaborations feels a little different.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

According to recent reports, there was a time when you could spot someone who had just finished a run. They were sweaty and wearing sneakers that looked like they belonged exclusively on a track. These days, the shoes tell you almost nothing. That guy wearing carbon-plated racers might be heading out for a tempo run, or he might just be on his way to a bar or running errands (in a casual fit).

Running shoes have officially entered their fashion era, and while the whole sneaker-meets-streetwear thing isn't exactly newly introduced (the chunky dad sneaker era still lives rent-free in my head), the latest wave of collaborations feels a little different. Instead of reviving old silhouettes, fashion brands are getting their hands on actual performance shoes, and, frankly, some of the results are pretty damn good.

Take Adidas' collaboration with Satisfy, the Parisian running brand that's become something of a cult favorite among runners who lowkey like to look good while out and about. Earlier this year, the two brands gave the Adizero Adios Pro 4 a makeover, swapping its usual racing aesthetic for earthy tones, spray-painted details, and metallic accents. At first glance, they look like something you could spot on an edgy Instagram campaign, perhaps even a fashion week after-party in Bushwick, depending on the outfit. Except, it's still a legitimate racing shoe with Lightstrike Pro foam and EnergyRods. You could absolutely chase a PR in these. Whether you'd want to get them dirty is another question. That’s just merely scraping the surface, though.

Highsnobiety's latest collaboration with Saucony takes a similar approach, but with two very different sneakers: the Endorphin Pro 5, made for racing, and the ProGrid Paramount, a retro-inspired shoe that's more at home on city streets. Both get a modest makeover that makes technical sneakers look good with practically anything. Some of you probably appreciate the distinction here: one shoe is built for runners, and the other is for people who strictly care about style.

In a recent development, then there's Hoka x Marni, which might be one of my favorites of the bunch. After giving the Bondi a ridiculously puffy, almost cartoonish makeover in 2025, the brands returned this November with the Clifton Marni, a more wearable take on Hoka's Clifton 11. There are metallic details, reflective accents, and a plaid sockliner, but underneath it all is still the cushioned daily trainer runners already know. It's stylish without looking like it's trying too hard, which can't be said for every designer sneaker collaboration.

Other brands have been getting in on the fun, too. Salomon and Pas Normal Studios recently put their spin on the Aero Blaze 4 GRVL, giving the gravel running shoe a sleek, outdoorsy look while keeping its GORE-TEX protection and trail-ready outsole. Aimé Leon Dore has brought its signature Upcoming York aesthetic to New Balance's FuelCell Rebel v5 and SC Elite v5, while Nike tapped designer Melitta Baumeister to reimagine the Vomero Premium and Pegasus Premium. Even Loewe and On are experimenting with high-fashion versions of technical running shoes. By now, the crossover is hard to ignore.

Of course, there's something funny about running, a sport that really doesn't require much beyond a decent pair of shoes (and your ability to actually run, of course), becoming another excuse to buy expensive, limited-edition sneakers. And not that this has to be mentioned, but a designer collaboration isn't automatically a better running shoe. The fit, cushioning, and performance still matter, especially if you're planning to do more than walk around in them. But I do think it's cool that brands are putting this much thought into how performance footwear looks. Running clothes have gotten a lot more stylish in recent years, so why shouldn't the shoes follow?

In a recent development, josiah Soto is a commerce editor and writer at Hearst Magazines, where he covers skincare, grooming, beauty, and style for Men’s Health, Prevention, and BestProducts.com. With a particular passion for skincare and the ingredients behind his favorite products, he keeps readers up to date on the latest beauty debuts, grooming essentials, and fashion trends worth knowing about. He also contributes to Runner’s World and Popular Mechanics, covering everything from emerging style trends to running gear and lifestyle products. In another life, Josiah was an editor at ThePioneerWoman.com.

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The first time I entered the Newly introduced York City Marathon drawing, I got in.
  • Industry observers note that my NYC Marathon training also happened during my senior year of college, which brought its own challenges.
  • Industry observers note that while training for those first few marathons, I didn’t have any real blueprint, except to not let it interfere with my social calendar.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The first time I entered the Newly introduced York City Marathon drawing, I got in. I’m not sure what possessed me that day to apply, having never run another race in my life. I figured I’d never get in, so why not? I played soccer growing up, and when the world shut down during COVID-19, running became the easiest way to get out of the house and see my friends. That’s where my running journey began.

Industry observers note that my NYC Marathon training also happened during my senior year of college, which brought its own challenges. While I was excited to run, I also didn’t want to miss out on any of the socializing that happened that year. I did my best to make it to every party, every club soccer game, and anything in between while running as much as possible. I was scared that running was going to infringe on my everyday life and I wouldn’t have time to keep having fun. Despite all of that, I had caught the marathon bug and after finishing the New York City Marathon in 2022, I went on to run the Paris and Chicago Marathons in 2024.

Industry observers note that while training for those first few marathons, I didn’t have any real blueprint, except to not let it interfere with my social calendar. My strategy consisted of building up mileage in order to reach 20 miles about four weeks out from race day. In between, I pieced together training information from influencers on Instagram and Google searches (this was pre-ChatGPT!). Now that I’m a Runner’s World+ member, I have all those resources right at my fingertips.

Recent findings suggest that although I caught the marathon bug almost instantly, I also felt defeated after New York. I knew I could have done better. Between New York City in 2022 and Paris in 2024, I never ran more than 10 miles at a time, but I was running enough that I knew I could do it again if I really wanted. I followed a similar approach for Chicago in 2024: Build up to one long run about a month out, then fill the rest of the weeks with shorter runs and one medium-length run. It wasn’t much of a plan, but it worked for me. My times kept improving, and I broke four hours for the first time in Chicago.

Sources indicate that looking back, I realize that my no-plan approach was partly a way to protect myself. If I never said my goal out loud, I couldn’t feel disappointed if I missed it. Breaking four hours in Chicago changed that. For the first time, I wanted to see what I could do with a real plan.

In a recent development, I was now living in the city I had expected to call home ever since I left college, so I really wanted this race to feel meaningful. For the first time in my marathon career, I downloaded a Runner’s World training plan, the 16-week Break 3:45 plan to be exact, printed it out, and started tracking all of my runs. I wanted to beat my time in Chicago and get as close to 3 hours and 45 minutes as possible.

In a recent development, in the beginning, this felt super daunting. I had never done an interval run in my life nor had I ever intentionally sought out hills to make my runs feel harder than they already did. Nonetheless, I found my old Garmin Forerunner 55 and learned how to upload intervals to run up and down the West Side Highway. When the plan called for hills, I made my way back to the Queensboro Bridge for the first time since 2022, ready to face it with excitement instead of fear. Even while pretending to be excited, the incline is no joke!

It has been revealed that for a while, I really felt like I had gotten the hang of things. I actually started to recognize what different paces felt like during the intervals, instead of sprinting and pulling back and looking at my watch while I ran. And, I could now confidently run over many of the bridges in New York City, notably the Williamsburg and Manhattan, even though they aren’t even part of the marathon course. I wasn’t following the strategy exactly, but I was able to reorganize the days of the week to hit all the workouts.

Industry observers note that this was working! Until it wasn’t.

Near the end of August (roughly week eight of the strategy), it became hot all the time, I was constantly traveling for weekend trips, and I had started to lose the excitement of running. So while I was making sure to hit all of the long runs, the interval training fell off completely. I was a little disappointed in myself because the interval training runs were workouts that made me feel like I was getting stronger each week. I had never done this type of workout before, so I could tell I was getting better each time.

Recent findings suggest that to find the joy of running again, I really started to lean on my friends. Every week, I’d send out a few texts to see who was available and wanted to go for a run with me. I ran the loop in Central Park almost every week and met up with my friends in Brooklyn to run every Friday morning. I started to explore parts of the city I had never been to before, which helped ground me in my training and remember that running is supposed to be fun and is an exciting way to explore the city.

From my previous experience, I knew that running the long runs was the most important thing for me to feel confident on race day. So much of marathon running is mental, so knowing that I could run 20 miles (and have run 26.2 before), was enough for me. So, while I started with a plan, I started reverting back to my tried-and-true method—the just make sure you run the long runs plan.

Sources indicate that outside of the training proposal itself, I leaned on Runner’s World a lot. I didn’t have access to this in the past so I didn’t feel confident about planning for prerun meals or even how to take gels during the race. I also found that being able to read runner stories online made me feel more connected to the community, which helped me mentally with my training.

Proposal or no plan, I’m proud of myself! My official time was 3:57:39, so while I did not achieve my goal of breaking 3:45, I did run a sub-4 race, and following the Runner’s World plan helped me get there. The last time I ran this race, I was a senior in college and thought I had it all figured out. I was going to move to New York City, get a real adult job, and start the life I had been imagining. Similar to my experience following the Runner’s World plan, this is not how everything went. Instead, I moved to a different city after graduating, eventually found my way back to New York, and my life is so much more full than I ever expected because of it. Maybe things aren’t always supposed to go to plan, and that’s a good thing!

The 7 Best Garmin Watches for Cyclists: Editor-Tested Picks for Training, Recovery, and Everyday Wear

📅 25 Mar 2022 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2138 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Cyclists, myself included, are often data driven.
  • Many riders and multisport athletes just don’t need a dedicated bike computer—especially with how smart smartwatches have become over the last few years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Cyclists, myself included, are often data driven. Even for cyclists that aren’t particularly motivated to optimize their performance there’s a belief that if a ride, run, hike, or any activity isn’t on Strava, it didn’t happen. Tracking your rides is easy to do with a head unit, but the tracking is limited to just the time spent on your bike.

Many riders and multisport athletes just don’t need a dedicated bike computer—especially with how smart smartwatches have become over the last few years. Smartwatches offer many of the same features that you find on bike computers, but smartwatches can also track sleep, heart rate, and activities you do off the bike. I have a few friends who even track mowing their lawn to make sure they don’t lose out on the activity for the day. With so many smartwatches out there, it can be hard to pick which one to choose, but time and again we go back to Garmin as the benchmark for tracking tech.

Industry observers note that tracking three back-to-back activities can be an annoyance for data-hungry triathletes. However, the Forerunner 970’s “Triathlon” mode gives multisport athletes the freedom to change between workouts without ending their activity. You only need to tap the lap button at the start and end of each transition. However, the 970 is a great option for folks who aren’t also swimming and running on their bike rides.

While I’m not a triathlete, I’ve been testing the 970 for a couple of weeks during road rides, commutes, and my daily routine; my overall impression is quite positive. This is a performance-optimized smartwatch for performance-minded athletes. It can track and measure seemingly every data point across an enormous range of sports and activities. Specifically related to cycling, the Forerunner 970 has preset profiles for: Road, mountain biking, gravel, commuting, touring, e-biking, eMTB riding, indoor, cyclocross, and BMX. If none of those options meet your niche, you can also create your own.

The variety and specificity of data you can track with the Forerunner 970 is mind-boggling. If you want to measure or see something related to riding, you probably can—although finding it in the array of options is sometimes the hardest part. And like Garmin’s head units, that’s the watch’s biggest downside. Garmin packs so many options into its devices that it can be difficult to navigate within the screens. Luckily, the Garmin Connect app is (mostly) easy to use, and changes made in the app instantly push to the phone.

It has been revealed that A feature I like on the 970 is the ability to “Lap by Location”. With this turned on, your watch will automatically start a upcoming lap each time you pass through that GPS location again. That means no more forgetting to tap “Lap” when you’re deep in the red zone with one lap to go in an event. This makes the 970 perfect for cyclocross, criterium, and XC mountain bike racers seeking to track in-race performance data at a granular level.

The Venu 4’s sleek, not-too-techy profile allows you to maximize your smartwatch mileage, both during workouts and in daily life. It prioritizes general smartwatch functionality, but there’s still plenty of processing power. That makes the Venu great for all-day wear, both on and off the bike.

Sources indicate that senior Art Director, Colin McSherry, has tested the Venu 4 against his trusty Forerunner. He notes the Venu‘s solid 12-day battery life is closer to 8 to 10 days when heavily using route navigation for cycling, running, and hiking. He also remarked, “I found the navigation a bit simpler and easier to use compared to the Garmin Forerunner 970 due to fewer physical buttons.”.

Sources indicate that on the bike, starting and tracking a workout is easy. McSherry noted that, “GPS does take a few seconds to register, but usually picks up as you are taking your first few pedal strokes.” Compared to his Wahoo Elemnt, he found the GPS data was very close. “So if I forgot my computer or wanted to get away from staring at a screen while on a ride, it’s a great way to track basic metrics,” he said.

Garmin released the Fēnix 9 this fall, but we still love the Fēnix 8—and there are some great deals on the watch right now. The 8 Pro is Garmin’s flagship model in its class-leading Fēnix lineup. This watch is packed with virtually every feature you could want to measure and manage your outdoor adventures. The Fēnix 8 Pro includes it all in a rugged design featuring dive-rated buttons, a crisp AMOLED display (or MicroLED for an extra $400), and a titanium bezel. The device connects via ANT+ or Bluetooth to third-party sensors and supports a wide range of activity profiles.

In a recent development, however, the Fēnix 8 Pro’s biggest upgrade is the included inReach satellite/LTE connectivity. (You previously needed a separate Garmin inReach device for that.) For backcountry adventurers, the ability to message, call, share location, or trigger SOS from your wrist is a must-have feature. All that capability comes at a cost—in both price and battery life. Garmin claims up to 15 days of battery life (in smartwatch mode) for the 47mm model and 27 days for the 51mm version. However, those numbers drop when LTE or satellite features are active.

In a recent development, jason Griffin, Senior Health and Fitness Editor, is currently testing the 8 Pro. He said, “It’s smarter than I expected a watch could be,” and notes that “answering calls through the watch is super easy, and tracking both rides and runs is intuitive.” He added, “The flashlight was great to find things in the middle of the night while I was holding my sleeping toddler.”.

While the Forerunner 265 is an older model, we find it strikes a good balance between Garmin’s budget-minded watches and its thousand-dollar devices. The 265’s accuracy is top-tier for its price, and this model has a far more readable display than its predecessor, thanks to a bright OLED screen—a near-critical feature if you don’t want to take your hands off your grips for too long to check your mileage.

If you have smaller wrists (or prefer a more compact watch), the Forerunner 265S is a great choice. It’s lighter, slimmer, and even offers longer battery life.

Recent findings suggest that garmin’s new Forerunner 70 isn’t really an patch of its long-running Forerunner 55 entry-level model: the 70 is an entirely new device. The new model has a larger display, tons more features, and (most importantly for cyclists) many more bicycle profile options.

The Forerunner 70 is designed to be a great running watch, and its features and data logging abilities are best for off-bike activities. However, the 70 is still a good option for fitness-minded riders or cyclists needing to log their rides and basic training data. So, while the 70 cannot connect to your power meter or smart trainer, it still features solid GPS tracking, a heart rate monitor, and it can follow pre-planned courses.

Buying Tip: If you need to track power, spend the extra $50 and upgrade to the Forerunner 170 model.

It has been revealed that garmin released the Enduro 4 this fall and we are right now testing it to see how it compares to the Enduro 3. The Enduro 3 is still a great option from Garmin and is on sale right now. The Enduro 3 is what happens when you take the top-shelf performance of the Fēnix and optimize it for maximum battery life. It’s a high-caliber solar watch that can last a staggering 36 days in smartwatch mode and up to 150 hours in GPS mode. It’s perfect for long bikepacking outings to places lacking spots to recharge.

At 51mm, the watch face is large but surprisingly unobtrusive. It feels light (63 grams) and comfortable on the wrist, even during long rides. The Enduro also has a sleeker profile than many premium smartwatches, with fewer sharp edges and oversized buttons. A feature our tester didn’t know they needed is the built-in flashlight. It works very well and is unexpectedly useful in everyday situations.

Industry observers note that while the Velcro strap may not win style points off the bike, it’s incredibly functional. It allows for a perfectly snug fit, unlike traditional watch bands (frequently, one loop is too tight and the next is too loose).

Industry observers note that garmin markets the Forerunner 170 Music as a running watch, but that label doesn’t do it justice. It’s a true multi-sport smartwatch, built to support a wide range of activities—including multiple cycling disciplines—and it connects to ANT+ and Bluetooth sensors for more detailed ride data and notifications.

Sources indicate that as the name suggests, it includes 4GB of onboard storage for music. This means you can leave your phone behind and still have your playlist. It also features an altimeter, barometer, compass (ABC sensors), a pulse oximeter, and advanced tracking tools, making it capable in almost any scenario.

Recent findings suggest that if you participate in various outdoor activities, you may prefer to own a single device to track everything. Whether cycling, running, hiking, paddling, walking the dog, or playing pickleball, a Garmin watch offers powerful, versatile functionality in a streamlined profile that’s always with you.

If you regularly track multiple types of workouts, while many road and gravel riders prefer cycling head units for instant access to maps, routing details, power metrics, and other data, some riders prefer smartwatches for logging ride data.

Sources indicate that not needing to learn or own multiple overlapping devices simplifies and declutters your life. And in his excellent story, “The Problem with Modern Cycling Computers Isn’t the Huge Screens,” Test Editor Dan Chabanov argues that many head units are bloated with unnecessary functions.

In a recent development, mountain bikers who often ride technical trails (bike park riders and enduro racers, for example) are increasingly turning to watches to document rides. With some cycling computers costing upwards of $1,000, you don’t want it dangling off the front of your bar or attached to your top tube in the event of a crash. Additionally, a computer is sometimes an unwanted distraction when trying to concentrate on a challenging descent.

Triathletes and duathlon racers are another group of riders who often prefer smartwatches. Watches allow athletes to transition between segments without needing to change devices or combine files after an event. Similarly, since the discipline involves swapping out muddy bikes in the pits during a race, cyclocross racers often use smartwatches.

In a recent development, A quick spin through Garmin’s website reveals a dizzying lineup of watches—sleek, feature-packed, and often overwhelming to sort through. While nearly all of them include the core functions you’d expect from a sports smartwatch, four series stand out as the best options for cyclists: Forerunner, Enduro, Fēnix, and Venu.

The Forerunner series is Garmin’s core watch for cyclists and multisport athletes. It includes five models, starting with the $250 Forerunner 70, which covers the basics, and going up to the $750 Forerunner 970, which combines high-end smartwatch features with advanced training and navigation tools.

The Enduro is designed for endurance athletes and offers the longest battery life of any Garmin watch. It includes the premium features of a cycling computer and smartwatch, along with extras such as solar charging and a built-in flashlight—making it a great option for long adventures.

Recent findings suggest that the Fēnix series shares many advanced features with the Enduro line—activity profiles, multisport tracking, and smartwatch tools—but adds specialized options for adventurers and divers. Fēnix has a slightly shorter battery life than the Enduro, and the watch faces are smaller.

Finally, the Venu is another option. It blends performance training, GPS, and data tracking features with fashion-forward styling. So, it looks good on and off the bike.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and Upcoming England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

#91717. Latest Update: The 12 Best Carbon Plate Shoes for Setting PRs, Running Your First Marathon, and Crossing the Finish Line Upright

Latest Update: The 12 Best Carbon Plate Shoes for Setting PRs, Running Your First Marathon, and Crossing the Finish Line Upright

📅 07 Jun 2023 | ⏱️ 20 min read (3950 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article.
  • There are several max-cushioned shoes we recommend to carry you through hours of pounding pavement, but the true titans—composed of super foams sandwiching carbon-fiber plates—are listed here.
  • Recent findings suggest that in 2017, Nike shook up running as we knew it with the unveiling of its Vaporfly 4%, a carbon plate marathon racing shoe that promised a 4 percent improvement in running economy (the measure of how fast you run based on the level of oxygen you use).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

There are several max-cushioned shoes we recommend to carry you through hours of pounding pavement, but the true titans—composed of super foams sandwiching carbon-fiber plates—are listed here. There’s also a slew of new super shoes that made their debut this marathon cycle. We’ll update accordingly once these racers are available.

Recent findings suggest that in 2017, Nike shook up running as we knew it with the unveiling of its Vaporfly 4%, a carbon plate marathon racing shoe that promised a 4 percent improvement in running economy (the measure of how fast you run based on the level of oxygen you use). Today, almost every shoe brand has a super shoe with a carbon plate and super foams, and they all make the same promise as the Vaporfly 4%: less energy expenditure while racing, or the ability to run faster with the same effort.

Industry observers note that here, we list the top performers based on wear-tester feedback and our own experiences racing in them. And if you’re in the market for other shoes to help you with your training, we have a buying guide for those too.

Your first marathon → Adidas Adizero Adios Pro 5 (Men’s/Women’s)For a PR → Nike Alphafly 4 (Men’s/Women’s)But want to train in a plated shoe → Fresh Balance SC Rebel (Men’s/Women’s)A flat and fast course → Saucony Endorphin Elite 3 (Unisex)A half marathon → Asics Metaspeed Edge Tokyo (Unisex)And want to try low drop → Altra Vanish Carbon 3 (Men’s/Women’s)And need support → Saucony Endorphin Pro 5 (Men’s/Women’s)And have wide feet → Hoka Cielo X1 3.0 (Unisex)On a track → Puma Fast-R Nitro Elite 3 (Men’s/Women’s)A 5K or 10K → New Balance SuperComp Elite v6 (Men’s/Women’s)On a trail → Hoka Tecton X 4 (Men’s/Women’s)An ultra → On Cloudultra Pro (Men’s/Women’s).

Industry observers note that besides our local testers, some of whom have been testing for us for the past 15 years, and staff who’ve also logged their share of road and trail time in these shoes, I have tested several of these shoes on race days. I have run 28 marathons since 2010, including 14 consecutive Boston Marathons. And I have made the split-second decision to race in new shoes marathon morning.

According to recent reports, I’ve spoken with brand shoe development teams and have kept up with the latest super shoe releases. New shoes not listed here are still undergoing the testing process and will be added once feedback is in.

All of the shoes on this list were tested by local runners and Runner’s World staff. Our local testers include 300-plus men and women of various running experience levels, paces, arch heights, and gait patterns. From enthusiasts who run for fun to several Olympic-qualifying hopefuls, our mix of testers rounds out a sample of the overall running pop.

RW editors, including myself, have also raced in these shoes, from 5K to marathon distance (and some ultrarunners). We take into consideration fit, feel, and ride to determine the best racing shoes for almost every kind of runner hoping to PR, or just enjoy the propulsive experience of running on carbon plates sandwiched between super foams.

According to recent reports, on a plane, running a shakeout run, and anytime a marathon was weeks away or days past, I’d hear first-timers and seasoned vets say the Adizero Adios Pro 4 was their race day shoe of choice. The latest iteration is sure to have the same mentions next race cycle.

Sources indicate that I didn’t have the chance to race in the Adizero Adios Pro 5 yet, but I did try them out on my usual Central Park circuit in Latest York City. I was practically racing my casual loop after slurping half a can of beer (it was a long day on the job). It obviously wasn’t the kiwi-flavored Belgian White that had me clocking marathon pace (it got kinda funky after the 25th sip).

Recent findings suggest that the carbon rim, which replaces the 4’s energy rods, is the secret sauce that subtracts weights and encourages a powerful snap that had me run up and down Harlem Hill like a gazelle. The Lightstrike Pro foam is also slightly firmer, which helps with high rebound and stability.

My only knock is how the rim shreds the hell of my ankle if my form gets slow and sloppy. But it’s a character trait. Senior Art Director Colin McSherry, for instance, ran his first marathon and had no complications—shoe- or first 26.2-related—during his run.

Shop Men’s at adidas.com | Shop Women’s at adidas.com.

Adidas Adizero Adios Pro 5 Review.

Industry observers note that the Alphafly 3 went through some major changes to become more inclusive in terms of fit, weight, and ride. How do you enhancement a shoe that was worn by the late Kelvin Kiptum, former marathon world record holder (2:00:35)? It starts with the Air units.

The ones in the Alphafly 4 are lighter and softer. During his testing, Runner-in-Chief Jeff Dengate noted how the unit visibly squishes down when you stomp on the forefoot. The effect is a smoother, comfier ride with lots of pop.

Sources indicate that the width of the shoe is also slightly wider (Nike really wants runners to stop saying their shoes are too unstable and narrow). Dengate noted how he didn’t have to slow down when turning corners.

The main critique is that loud clomping sound. But at this point—is it really an Alphafly if you can’t hear it coming up from behind you meters away?

Shop Men’s at nike.com | Shop Women’s at nike.com.

Industry observers note that the jury is still out on the pros and cons of solely training in super shoes, but we’re in the camp of keeping your special trainer fresh for race day. You can get a couple of runs in to troubleshoot and see if there are any issues pre-marathon or half, but I still urge runners to save the magic. But if you can’t get enough of that super foam, carbon plate high, enter the SC Rebel.

Recent findings suggest that upcoming Balance created this shoe specifically to make your training feel easier. It has the brand’s new TPEE-based Infinion foam, tuned for power runs, just like the SuperComp Elite v6 (New Balance’s premium racing shoe). It’s also an ideal alternative for racing if you need more stability. The shoe has a broader platform and grippy outsole that kept me upright on wet mud during a long run.

Shop Men’s at newbalance.com | Shop Women’s at newbalance.com.

New Balance SuperComp Rebel Review.

The Endorphin Elite 3 is as squishy and bouncy as its predecessor, but Saucony made the shoe more stable by connecting the forefoot and heel. Turns are less scary, but there’s still a learning curve to master the incredible energy return running in these shoes.

According to recent reports, I tested them at a 5K and 3K in the Brooklyn Navy Yard, which was pocked with potholes and patched with slippery gravel. The shoes cut corners, but I still felt the need to slow down—or wipe out. I think on a more controlled runner’s feet these would make her feel powerful and unbeatable.

The source of that aggressive bounce is the TPEE-based IncrediRun foam. Its ride rivals even PEBA’s energy return.

In a recent development, the shoe also didn’t produce hot spots in the toe area. Saucony seems to have improved the fit with the third version. Once I wield this shoe’s power I won’t be afraid to run longer than a 10K. No friction here.

Shop Endorphin Elite 3 at saucony.com.

Saucony Endorphin Elite 3 Review.

Recent findings suggest that when I ran the Tokyo Marathon last year, I laced up in the Asics Metaspeed Sky Paris because I wanted more cushioning in the forefoot area. Asics recognized there are two ways of racing: stride running or cadence running. The Sky is intended for stride running: when you have a more powerful gait with longer strides and tend to strike on the midfoot.

At the Sydney Marathon this year, I opted for the Metaspeed Edge Tokyo instead. I felt the Edge would give me the, er, competitive edge, so to speak. My steps per minute are usually more than the average runner due to my mechanics and, well, because I’m short. The shoe has a scooped plate tilted slightly downward to cater to those with shorter steps (cadence running). I ended up hitting my sub-3:10 goal, finishing in 3:05.

The Edge Tokyo is updated with a softer underfoot, making the shoe more flexible. This makes the shoe have an incredible snap at toe-off. I was able to change gears at a fast clip when I latched onto a runner I was determined to pass (not always the best race strategy, but worked like a charm when I saw male runners try to overtake me).

Recent findings suggest that where competitors’ shoes have “air pods” or decoupled heels, the Metaspeeds provide runners with a simplified, choose-your-own-adventure super shoe that packs a powerful punch. One note for the wise: Because the Edge Tokyo has less firm cushioning, my heels and arches felt sore postrace. If you have heavy footfalls like me, have those recovery sandals waiting for you at bag check.

Shop Asics Metaspeed Edge Tokyo at amazon.com.

Asics Metaspeed Tokyo Shoes Review.

Industry observers note that altra started its journey into super shoes by staying true to itself. The Vanish Carbon 1 and 2 had wide toeboxes and were zero drop. But the Altra team knew there would have to be a compromise to go up against competitors’ shoes: the Vanish Carbon 3 needed a drop. The brand preserved the Altra way by adding just 4 mm (like the shoes in its Experience collection) to the heel with an aggressive rocker profile to promote propulsion.

Another Altra signature in the shoe is the roomy toebox that gives racers space to splay their toes, allowing them to engage their digits and power up during push-off.

Recent findings suggest that the third iteration has pure PEBA midsole foam called FastRce. The foam provides more energy return and 2.6 percent improved running economy over the Vanish Carbon 2, which had a PEBA/EVA blend in its midsole.

The overall package presents a racer capable of racing against the other super shoes on this list.

Shop Women’s at altrarunning.com.

The Endorphin Pro 5 has a more stable ride than its springier sibling, the Endorphin Elite 2, which we also included on this list.

Sources indicate that its midsole is dual-layer PEBA, with one layer Pwrrun PB and the other layer Pwrrun HG. These layers provide a high-rebound ride and work with the rocker Speedroll tech to encourage fast, smooth turnover.

Testers like the shoe’s propulsive ride as well as support throughout their workouts.

Sources indicate that “What stood out most was the combination of propulsion and stability,” said tester Srah Pezzino. “The carbon plate paired with Saucony’s Pwrrun HG foam delivers a responsive, fast ride without feeling unstable or overly bouncy. This helped immensely during longer tempo runs when fatigue starts to creep in. I felt like the shoe encouraged good mechanics and smooth turnover rather than forcing speed.

Industry observers note that “Compared to previous carbon-plated shoes I’ve worn, the Pro 5 feels more predictable and controlled, especially when my form isn’t perfect late in a run. It’s a shoe that makes you feel fast without punishing you for not being perfectly locked in.”.

Shop Men’s at saucony.com | Shop Women’s at saucony.com.

Sources indicate that the lightest Hoka marathon racing shoe yet is the Cielo X1 3.0, with street cred at the 2025 Chicago Marathon. Hoka-sponsored pro-runner Alex Masai raced in a blacked-out prototype of the shoe, shaved nearly four minutes off his personal best time, and podiumed third with a 2:04:37 finish.

Sources indicate that and our testers clocked the shoe’s massive updates, as well. “The 3.0 is sturdier than the 2.0,” mentioned tester Mike Browne. “I’m referring to the sturdiness mainly on heel strikes. I wore the 2.0 during marathon training and in a marathon, and they actually underpronated a little. I think that is what caused the outside heel rubber to come off on both shoes. The 3.0 has corrected that glitch and seems to strike the ground in the center, which makes for a more even wear on the shoe.”.

It has been revealed that besides implementing a lighter upper, the Hoka team redesigned the midsole shape, creating a long channel that runs down the center of the shoe. The rocker also isn’t as exaggerated. What you get is a more stable, smoother ride while racing with propulsion that’s comparable to Hoka’s competitors’. The fit is also broader in the midfoot, making the Cielo X1 3.0 a good choice for runners with wide feet.

Shop Hoka Cielo X1 3 at hoka.com.

Industry observers note that the Fast-R Nitro Elite 3 is a prime pick for marathon racing, but it’s also a solid choice for everything else under 26.2 miles. The shoe is so lightweight and delivers such explosive rebound—“you feel like you’re running straight down a trampoline,” says a tester—that it left some of us feeling like we had brownie batter for legs after hard efforts.

Recent findings suggest that the shoe was the talk of the industry prelaunch after Puma released a study (which the brand sponsored) comparing the Fast-R Nitro Elite 3’s performance to the Nike Alphafly 3, Adidas Adios Pro Evo 1, and Puma Fast-R 2. The study claimed the Elite 3 was 3.15 to 3.62 percent more economical than its competitors.

Putting those numbers aside, our testers agreed this is one powerful racing shoe. “The foam used in this shoe is very noticeable, even when simply starting with a short warmup in the shoe,” claims tester Codi Januszkiewicz, who compares the ride to the Adidas Adizero Adios Pro 4. “Accelerating from a warmup pace straight into some speedwork intervals felt smooth; somehow moving faster in this shoe felt even easier than the warmup.”.

It has been revealed that but that power is a lot to handle. “The stability is lacking,” states tester Sean O’Connor. “Almost felt high heelish to me, and it jacked up my calves and feet a little as well. When I ran in them it felt like I was perpetually holding onto the shoe with my feet. I think that's why it made my calves and feet sore.”.

Industry observers note that some can handle the shoe’s intensity over a long period of time. Others may assign the Elite 3 as their mid-distance racing shoe instead. I wore the Elite 3 at a Trackmith 5000 meters over the summer, hitting a PR at 19:12. It’s cush in the heel, but judging by my footfalls, which are heavy, I think racing them in a 26.2 would prolong my usual recovery time postrun.

When I raced the 2025 London Marathon, I had been training in the FuelCell SuperComp Elite v4 but instead opted for the FuelCell SuperComp Pacer v2. The Pacer is sleeker and lightweight, unlike the SuperComp Elite v4, which was too beefy for my small frame. The SuperComp Elite v6 is the version of the shoe I would have raced in. Unfortunately, I can’t go back to April 2025. Fortunately for you, the Elite v6 is here just in time for fall marathon season.

It has been revealed that the shoe features the brand’s Infinion foam, which was introduced in the 1080v15. The Elite v6’s version of the TPEE- and TPU-based foam is dialed-in for race-ready energy return.

I took the shoe out on a track for a 2 x 2-mile workout at 6:45 pace and the shoes handled turns and helped me hit goal pace. The ride isn’t as aggressive as the Saucony Endorphin Elite 3 or Alphafly, and the cushioning is firmer. Runners with an efficient stride and good form can get away with running marathons and halfs in these shoes, but I’d recommend these for 5Ks and 10Ks because of the firmness and less explosive rebound. The lighter weight makes it ideal for track and medium-distance road races.

Shop Men’s at newbalance.com | Shop Women’s at newbalance.com.

New Balance SuperComp Elite v6 Review.

According to recent reports, though I’ve been racing for 20 years, nothing will get me running an ultra on the trail—which is where our Senior Editor Cat Bowen comes in. Bowen conquered scrambles on steep climbs, dusty ridgelines, gnarly technical trails, and more types of terrain than I run in a year, while testing the long-awaited Tecton X 4.

In a recent development, she gave a shoutout to the hardy Matryx upper that’s “tough as nails” and the grippy 4mm lugs that prevented her from plunging forward. The plus/minus with the shoe is that built-in gaiter collar. Bowen appreciated the extra coverage, but lamented how difficult it was to put on the shoe (we get it: a side zipper would be a good cheat but adds weight). “There is absolutely no reason why this shoe has a front pull tab and nothing in the back,” she wrote in her review.

Industry observers note that still, the new cushioning, Hoka’s ProFly X, and non-winged plate make for a more energized ride that’s less rigid without losing stability. It’s a great shoe for unpredictable. but Bowen urges you to not go the no-sock route.

Shop Men’s at hoka.com | Shop Women’s at hoka.com.

In a recent development, for hours, days, weeks on the trail, there’s the Cloudultra Pro. Bowen has gone through three pairs of the shoe—not because they lack durability but because she likes them so much and runs that much—and appreciates how she doesn’t have to slice the sides. Feet swell during ultras, but it sounds like On prepared for that with its roomy but secure upper.

Industry observers note that another plus in Bowen’s column of ultra shoe musts is the Cloudultra Pro’s lateral stability. Maneuvering over rugged, uneven terrain could spell twisted ankles and slipping and sliding, but the shoe didn’t lead Bowen astray.

Ultrarunner Pat Heine-Holmberg also wore the shoe around Germany’s Zugspitze, where he raced the 102-mile ZUT1000 and ran on “every surface imaginable.”.

Shop Men’s at on.com | Shop Women’s at on.com.

Recent findings suggest that brands are now beginning to release carbon shoes in men’s and women’s sizes. Still, in some cases there’s not much difference between the types of shoes except for maybe the sizing and colors. If the shoes are unisex, it may take a few try-ons to get the fit right. In my unisex racing shoe experience, I’ve found the collar can be loose while the midfoot can be tight. You may want to size up or down, and adopt the heel-lock tying method if the heel area feels too loose.

Do all carbon-fiber plates behave the same way? Sort of. An key lesson to learn here is that the plate isn’t the secret sauce of super shoes—it doesn’t cause propulsion. Instead, the plate, sandwiched between the highly responsive foams, acts as a stabilizer to the super foam. This is why super shoes have such tall stack heights, and why World Athletics caps racing shoe stack height at 40 mm. The super foam—and amount underfoot—is a major advantage.

When choosing a carbon-plate shoe, you’ll want to consider what you’re using it for—racing on the road or trail—and, if possible, have your gait evaluated to determine the best plate angle if you’re looking at shoes specific to running type.

Some plates are full-length or have cutouts. In shoes like the Asics Metaspeed Edge and Metaspeed Sky, the plate’s angle differentiates running types. The Edge’s plate dips lower in the forefoot so cadence runners can roll off their toes faster. The Sky’s plate sits flat in the forefoot, allowing stride runners to leverage bounce on longer steps.

According to recent reports, the secret sauce in super shoes is the foam. PEBA (polyether block amide) was once considered the holy grail of all foams and you can still find it in most super shoes, but newer models are using TPEE (thermoplastic polyester elastomer) and A-TPU (aliphatic thermoplastic polyurethane) because they’re more resistant to bottoming out, or going flat. The ride is more durable—and can be quite aggressively bouncy and squishy.

To truly gauge which foam is best for you, trying on the shoe and giving it a run (preferably with some cornering) will help you determine if you want a firmer or squishier ride.

According to recent reports, A carbon-fiber plate shoe is an investment, costing anywhere from $240 upward of $500. There are a couple of things to take into account on a personal level before buying: Can you afford a trainer that’s less durable compared to the standard workhorse shoe, which lasts between 450 to 500 miles?

In a recent development, while these super shoes are more durable than the ones made eight years ago, they still have a shorter shelf life due to high-performance foams—PEBA and supercritical blends—wearing down faster. Lastly, is the return there? While brands claim these shoes can improve performance, it’s not guaranteed your running economy will improve by around 4 percent.

Recent findings suggest that I spoke with Ted Fitzpatrick, Saucony’s VP of product management, about the differences. He made these key points between carbon and nylon plates:.

It has been revealed that A nylon plate is semirigid with some flexibility. A carbon plate is rigid with little or no flexibility. Popsicle analogy—Imagine the plate as the stick that holds the soft ice cream together. The fundamental use of the plates is to keep the dimensional stability of the foam. With each type of plate, each offers different levels of compliance. The plate maintains the forward rolling effect of super shoes. Carbon is the stiffest, which offers the most concentrated effect of speed roll technology. Nylon still adds stiffness, however, it offers better compliance in how the foot transitions in the gait cycle. Some individuals can respond better to different plates. It is down to what works best for the user.

It has been revealed that saucony offers the nylon-plated Endorphin Speed 6, a training shoe that complements its racer, the Endorphin Pro. The shoe can also serve as a more affordable racing shoe, at $180. (The Endorphin Elite 3 and Endorphin Pro 5 cost $290 and $240.).

“The foam is what does the heavy lifting of a super shoe, however it’s the plate that guides how each foam behaves to the user,” notes Fitzpatrick. “It is best to train in both to strengthen and build ‘muscle memory’ into different muscle groups.”.

Sources indicate that however, we wouldn’t recommend solely training in super shoes. For one thing, it would be extremely expensive to use these shoes as daily trainers when they have a shorter shelf life compared to standard everyday shoes. We advise going on a couple of runs before racing in the shoes, to get used to running in them and check for hot spots. While running constantly in these shoes won’t necessarily lead to injury, overuse and the desire to run faster in carbon shoes will likely lead to getting sidelined if you’re not careful.

Amanda Furrer, Editor, Running Reviews, studied journalism at NYU and writing at Emerson College. She has reviewed gear and covered other topics in the running space for almost 10 years. Since 2013, she has consecutively run the Boston Marathon. She also has a master’s degree in gastronomy from Boston University and was formerly a professional baker for two years before hanging up her apron.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that glute bridge post-run.
  • For this article, physical therapist Jennie Hansen analyzed a upcoming study on anti-movement vs.
  • Industry observers note that “Core strengthening” is a term runners frequently toss around.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that glute bridge post-run. (Photo: Aleksandr Kondratov, Getty).

For this article, physical therapist Jennie Hansen analyzed a upcoming study on anti-movement vs. dynamic core training and built a simple, science-backed core routine for runners based on the findings. The routine targets the deep stabilizing muscles that protect your spine and improve performance.

Industry observers note that “Core strengthening” is a term runners frequently toss around. We all know we need it. But what exactly is it, and what should it entail? (Hint: Not crunches.).

Industry observers note that when we talk about the core, we mean the abdominal muscles, low back, gluteal, pelvic, and hip muscles that support the spine and trunk. These muscles include both smaller, deep groups that attach directly to the spine to provide stabilization and larger, more global ones that can assist with stability and produce movement.

In a recent development, why do we need this area to be strong? Well, even non-runners need to pay attention to their core strength to avoid lower back pain, which is the top cause of years lived with disability. Athletically, the core must create proximal stability to allow for powerful, efficient movements distally—which requires adequate strength combined with coordinated neuromuscular activation and control. So, core strength is certainly crucial for pain reduction, injury prevention, and athletic performance.

Industry observers note that when running, the trunk serves to provide a stable base of support so that the legs can effectively generate the forces that create forward movement. These forces are transferred across the trunk and counterbalanced by the arms, requiring coordination between the hips, trunk muscles, and shoulders.

According to recent reports, while running appears to be purely a forward (sagittal plane) activity, the trunk muscles are hard at work controlling side-to-side (frontal plane) and rotational (transverse plane) forces. Muscle activation and timing change with speed, with higher speeds generally requiring more control and work. The deep trunk muscles also contribute to respiration.

While some small trunk motion naturally occurs with running, excessive motion is detrimental. Increased trunk flexion is associated with decreased running economy and increased loading rates and vertical impact forces. Increased lateral trunk lean has also been linked to increased loading rates, which may play a role in the development of certain injuries.

Even though most of us know that crunches are out, there’s still plenty of confusion about how to train our cores. While strength work doesn’t need to look exactly like running, it does need to meet (and exceed) its demands—meaning that stability should be emphasized over motion.

It has been revealed that enter a recent study comparing neuromuscular activation between “anti-movement” and “dynamic” core training. Unlike traditional dynamic core exercises, which work the trunk and spinal musculature by moving through flexion, extension, rotation, and side bending, anti-movement exercises resist external forces, forcing stabilization throughout the trunk—basically, trunk isometrics.

The 12-week study compared a combination of Pallof holds and plank variations (incorporating bands and the TRX suspension trainer for progression) in the anti-movement program against a dynamic program that included exercises such as sit-ups, leg raises, jack knives, Russian twists, windshield wipers, and back extensions (incorporating Swiss balls for progression).

While both exercise groups demonstrated enhancements in neuromuscular efficiency compared to a control group, improvements were overall greater in the anti-movement group, particularly within the deep local musculature that activates prior to limb movement and plays an vital role in stabilizing the spine.

The authors therefore hypothesized that this enhanced neuromuscular efficiency could improve endurance, delay fatigue, and reduce the need for recruitment of larger, more global muscles—thus protecting the spine and potentially decreasing injury risk while improving performance.

In a recent development, runners can apply these findings and consider an “anti-movement”-focused core routine, similar to the one used in the study. Nothing fancy or extensive is required—just one exercise each to resist the trunk’s motions (flexion, extension, rotation, and side-bending/lateral flexion). Simple plank variations and other holds work well to streamline your core routine efficiently and effectively.

Targets: Anti-extension · full core (local and global).

The front plank is a classic core stability exercise that falls into the anti-extension category, challenging most of both the local and global core muscles.

Targets: Anti-flexion · spinal extensors and glutes.

While the study used a supine plank as its anti-flexion exercise, the shoulder position required could be a limiter, so bridge holds are likely a more practical way for many runners to work the posterior trunk muscles, including the spinal extensors and gluteals.

Targets: Anti-lateral flexion · lateral trunk and hip muscles.

The side plank can be considered an anti-lateral-flexion exercise, challenging the lateral trunk and hip musculature.

Targets: Anti-rotation · obliques and deep abdominal rotators.

The Pallof press is a common anti-rotation exercise, challenging the deep abdominal rotators, including the obliques.

## Flying Qatar QSuites for 70,000 Miles: The Redemption That Feels Impossible Until You Do It Imagine settling into your own private suite — a door that actually closes, a fully flat bed measuring 80 inches long, a 21.5-inch 4K screen, and a meal service that rivals the best business-class restaurants at 40,000 feet. Qatar Airways QSuites isn't just the best business class product in the sky right now; it's the product that frequent flyers describe as the moment they understood why people obsess over travel rewards. And you can book it for 70,000 American AAdvantage miles one-way. Let that sink in. The same seat — Washington Dulles to Doha, with the ability to continue to dozens of destinations across Asia, Africa, and beyond — retails for **$5,000 to $9,000 in cash**. At 70,000 AAdvantage miles, you're extracting between **7.1 and 12.9 cents per point**. The ChooseFI community benchmarks a "good" redemption at 1.5 to 2 cents per point. This redemption is *three to six times that*. This is what the FI community means when we talk about travel rewards as a genuine wealth multiplier. If you've been stockpiling points wondering whether they're actually worth something, this is your answer. A cash ticket that costs more than many people's monthly take-home salary becomes nearly free with the right points strategy. The inefficiency exists because AAdvantage still prices partner awards — flights on airlines like Qatar, JAL, and Cathay Pacific — on a **fixed partner award chart** rather than the dynamic pricing it uses for American-operated flights. Qatar, as a oneworld alliance member, is required to make award space available to partner programs. American prices that space at a flat 70,000 miles for business class, regardless of what Qatar itself charges in cash or its own Avios currency. The result is a structural arbitrage opportunity: you're using a fixed-price chart to book a premium product that Qatar prices at whatever the market will bear — and the market bears a *lot* for QSuites. The ChooseFI community has long understood that the highest-leverage use of points isn't domestic economy upgrades. It's premium international cabin redemptions where the gap between cash price and points cost is widest. On that spectrum, QSuites via AAdvantage sits near the very top.

In a recent development, the core insight here is understanding two separate pricing systems operating simultaneously. Qatar Airways prices its QSuites cabin dynamically in cash — demand surges around holidays, business travel seasons, and major events can push that $5,000 base price to $9,000 or beyond. But American AAdvantage doesn't care about any of that. As a oneworld alliance partner, AAdvantage uses a fixed partner award chart for Qatar redemptions: 70,000 miles one-way in business class, full stop.

It has been revealed that this means the more expensive the cash ticket gets, the better your CPP becomes — without you doing anything differently. Book during peak travel periods when cash prices spike to $9,000, and you're extracting 12.9 cents per AAdvantage mile. Even at the floor — a $5,000 cash ticket — you're at 7.1 cents per point. Both numbers are extraordinary.

AAdvantage periodically runs "Web Specials" — discounted partner awards where pricing drops significantly below the standard chart. Latest Update: My Shimano Pedals Are Nearly 10 Years Old—This 10-Minute Service Saved Me From Spending $200 on a New Set

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

My longest-lasting pedals are a roughly 10-year-old pair of Shimano SPD XT pedals that have admittedly seen zero maintenance. Those pedals have been effectively abused on everything from getting bashed through rock gardens to long dusty or muddy days on the gravel bike. A few years ago I got my first road bike and switched to a pair of Shimano SPD-SL pedals. Since then I’ve put that bike (and those pedals) through the wringer.

I tend to stress test gear, even prior to having this job, so I enjoy taking my road bike out on everything from light gravel to singletrack that I have no business on. This means my road pedals have seen similar abuse to my mountain bike and gravel pedals. They’re still in great shape, but they could use a little love. Even pedals only used for road riding will start to get gritty over time.

Then I saw Shimano’s pedal release—not only are the old cleats not compatible with the newly introduced pedals, but the price of the new Shimano pedals starts at $200 for the Ultegra model and go up to $300 for the Dura-Ace model.

Recent findings suggest that after I saw the rollout, it felt like a good time to bring my old generation SPD-SL pedals back to life and while I’m at it, give you a few tips on the process. Here we’ll run through how to service your SPD-SL pedals in under 10 minutes and save you a few hundred dollars in the process.

According to recent reports, A quick note on reinstalling the pedals back on the bike: make sure you put the right pedal on the right side and the left pedal on the left side. I know, this sounds obvious. I’ve seen the wrong pedal get forced into the wrong side of the crank too many times, damaging the crank and the pedals to the point that sometimes both need to be replaced. Sometimes pedals are marked with an “L” for left and “R” for right, but you can always double-check to see which way the threads go. Left pedal threads will go up to the left and right pedal threads go up to the right. Then when it is time to reattach the pedals, put some grease on the threads of the crank arm and begin to thread them on by hand instead of starting with the wrench. If you can’t begin to thread the pedal onto the crank threads by hand, double-check the pedal is on the correct side, make sure it’s going into the crank arm straight, and make sure there is no debris in the hole of the crank arm preventing it from threading.

Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.

Breaking: The 9 Best Stability Shoes for Every Type of Runner

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
